We also need to talk about skill and difficulty.

Difficulty alone is not what makes games like Dark Souls or Elden Ring (and indeed, the first Hollow Knight game) good. Those games are specifically designed to give the player very straight-forward ways to compensate for lack of mechanical skill.

They make sure that the player has some way to increase their character power and then come back to a difficult fight if the player's skill alone is insufficient. This is a good thing, because not every player possesses very high mechanical skill or is interested in grinding the same boss for 5 hours. text:
A great boss rush hidden inside a frustrating game

I really wanted to love Silksong. I’m a huge fan of Hollow Knight, and after spending a lot of time with Silksong, I can say that its boss design is genuinely excellent. Unfortunately, the rest of the game repeatedly gets in the way of that.

What works

Bosses are by far the strongest part of the game.

The best fights — Lace, Widow, Moorwing, Fourth Chorus, Trobbyo and the Last Judge — are difficult but fair. Attacks are well telegraphed, patterns can be learned, and deaths usually feel like “I screwed up” rather than “the game screwed me.”

The best fights have exactly the kind of difficulty I enjoy: you die, understand something new, immediately try again, and eventually beat the boss because you actually improved.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 233368212

text:
The best fights have exactly the kind of difficulty I enjoy: you die, understand something new, immediately try again, and eventually beat the boss because you actually improved.

The movement also gets significantly better as you unlock abilities such as dash, cloak glide, wall cling and downward strike. At that point the platforming starts to feel much more fluid and intuitive — and it becomes obvious that many areas were probably designed around these abilities from the beginning.

The visual and thematic design is also fantastic. Trobbyo, for example, is an excellent concept: a performer who never left his role, with attacks based around the stage, dance, fireworks, smoke and spectacle. The game is full of this kind of creativity.

What doesn't work

Unfortunately, the game constantly wastes my time between the good parts.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 233368212

text:
Unfortunately, the game constantly wastes my time between the good parts.

The biggest problem for me is the level design around difficult encounters. Long runbacks, huge empty areas, tedious platforming sections and mandatory enemy gauntlets often make reaching a boss more frustrating than actually fighting it.

A difficult boss with a 15-second runback? Great.

A difficult boss after several minutes of already-mastered platforming and combat? Exhausting.

The game also has a serious problem with regular enemies. They become increasingly tanky without becoming more interesting. Eventually I stopped learning their movesets and simply spammed attacks, because deliberately fighting them was slower and, ironically, less safe than just trading damage and healing afterwards. When the optimal strategy is to ignore or mindlessly facetank enemies rather than engage with the combat system, something feels wrong with the balance.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 233368212

text:
The two-currency system is another major annoyance. Different enemies drop different currencies, one has a hard cap, and useful things constantly require the currency you don't currently have. It feels less like an interesting economy and more like a system designed to make you spend more time grinding.

The health system also feels poorly balanced. You can have five masks, yet many enemies and environmental hazards deal two masks of damage. This makes some upgrades feel strangely unrewarding.

And then there are the minions. Some bosses use additional flying enemies in a way that turns otherwise manageable fights into chaotic RNG. When a boss is fun but an unpredictable flying enemy randomly collides with your dodge or attack, the fight stops feeling like a skill test.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 233368212

text:
The biggest problem

The frustrating part is that Silksong clearly knows how to make fantastic difficult gameplay.

When the game gives me a boss, a short runback and a readable moveset, I can happily die ten times and keep thinking:

“One more try.”

When the game gives me a long enemy gauntlet, platforming, environmental hazards and no checkpoint, I start thinking:

“Why am I wasting my time doing this again?”

That distinction ultimately killed the game for me.

I don't mind difficult games. I don't even mind extremely difficult games. I mind difficulty created by making me repeat content I have already mastered.

I eventually reached a section with an enemy arena dealing two-mask damage, followed by a lava escape/platforming sequence, without a meaningful checkpoint. At that point I simply stopped playing.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 233368212

text:
At that point I simply stopped playing.

The irony is that I don't think Silksong is too difficult. I think it is too willing to waste the player's time.

There is an excellent combat/boss game buried inside a beautiful but frequently exhausting metroidvania.

Great bosses. Great art. Great movement once upgraded.
Too much grind, too many tanky enemies, too many long runbacks, and too much repetition.

For me, unfortunately, the frustration eventually outweighed the fun.

I have very conflicted feelings about Silksong...
On one hand, it is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played, with an incredible soundtrack and a lovingly crafted world dripping with atmosphere, whose stories I wanted to see unfold.

There is no such thing as a "casual Silksong playthrough" - it expects you to *lock in* and master its mechanics, or suffer (perhaps both). text:
Hollow Knight: Silksong is a sequel that I had frankly a lot of expectations for, and if I am honest… This game exceeded all the expectations I had.

Story-wise, one thing I instantly noticed is how much more present the story feels during gameplay. While I’m not entirely sure how to explain it, but the best way I can describe it is that it feels like you always have a certain goal in mind, and that goal constantly shifts as you progress. Now, this is a goal largely set by yourself, so it can be quite personal, but I personally felt like I always had some idea of what I was searching for or what I was working towards.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text:
It made the story feel more integrated into the actual gameplay than it did in Hollow Knight. Hornet also feels much more alive as a protagonist. Obviously, a large part of this comes from the fact that she actually speaks, unlike the Knight, but I think there is more to it than that.

Atmosphere-wise, I think Silksong stands just as tall as Hollow Knight, if not slightly higher. The locations throughout Pharloom feel much more alive, which creates a noticeable contrast with Hollow Knight. In that game, Hallownest was intentionally designed as a fallen and decaying kingdom, so much of its atmosphere revolved around ruin, isolation, and the remnants of a world that had already collapsed.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text: Pharloom, by comparison, feels far more active and inhabited, giving its environments a greater sense of vitality. Detailed background lighting, sharper animations, and a more dynamic audio design all contribute to this. Traversing through Pharloom feels more reactive. These elements make the environments feel more like living spaces that exist independently of the player that it did in Hollow Knight. Personally, I prefer the atmosphere of Silksong over the original, but I think this ultimately comes down to personal preference. The two games are clearly going for different atmospheric identities: Hollow Knight embraces a melancholic, decaying world, while Silksong leans more toward something vibrant, animated, and constantly in motion yet still quite melancholic.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text:
Gameplay-wise, Silksong is a massive step above Hollow Knight for me. Hollow Knight already has incredibly satisfying movement, but the Knight generally feels more grounded. His movement is deliberate, and while abilities such as Mantis Claw, Monarch Wings, and Crystal Dash give him considerable mobility, they often feel more like tools for navigating the world than direct extensions of his combat style. Hornet, by comparison, feels as though her entire moveset has been designed around movement and momentum.
One of the biggest additions in Silksong is the Tool system, which feels far more active and gameplay-focused than Hollow Knight’s Charms. In Hollow Knight, Charms primarily modify the Knight’s existing abilities, affecting things such as damage, spell efficiency, movement, or healing.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text:
In Hollow Knight, Charms primarily modify the Knight’s existing abilities, affecting things such as damage, spell efficiency, movement, or healing. Tools, by comparison, feel much more like actual pieces of equipment that you actively incorporate into your gameplay. Rather than simply altering how Hornet’s abilities function, they can give her entirely new ways to attack, defend herself, or interact with enemies.
What I particularly appreciate about Tools is how much more connected they make preparation to your actual playstyle. A Tool isn’t simply a passive bonus that you equip and then forget about. Many of them provide abilities that you can deliberately activate during combat, effectively making your equipment another component of your moveset. This creates a much greater distinction between different playstyles, because changing your Tools can fundamentally alter how you approach an encounter rather than simply making the same strategy slightly more effective.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text:
Another particularly interesting addition is the Crest system. Crests essentially function as different loadouts that can fundamentally change the way Hornet plays. Rather than simply providing passive bonuses like Charms, different Crests can alter aspects of her moveset, attacks, and overall combat style.
Then there are Silk Skills. These are special abilities that give Hornet additional ways to utilize her silk during combat. What makes them particularly interesting is how distinct they are from one another, giving you a variety of active abilities that you can incorporate into your playstyle.
Now all I said is mostly scratching the surface of the difference in gameplay and I truly think that gameplay wise, this game is miles better than Hollow Knight
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235891602

text:
Overall, Hollow Knight: Silksong takes everything that made the original special and expands upon it in meaningful ways. Its story feels more integrated into the gameplay, giving Hornet a stronger sense of purpose as she moves through Pharloom. The atmosphere is just as impressive, trading Hallownest’s decaying isolation for a more vibrant, active, and living world without losing the melancholic ton. Most importantly, the gameplay feels like a major evolution, with Hornet’s movement, Tools, Crests, and Silk Skills creating far more depth and freedom in both exploration and combat.
While Hollow Knight remains an incredible game, Silksong feels like a genuine step forward rather than simply a bigger version of its predecessor. If you enjoyed Hollow Knight or simply love challenging Metroidvania games, Hollow Knight: Silksong is a must-buy.

text:
TL;DR: Great game, worse Hollow Knight. 8/10

For context: the original Hollow Knight is my favorite game of all time. I've beaten it deathless and without upgrading my character. So when I say Silksong frustrated me, it's not a skill issue rant.

If Hollow Knight gives you a wall and tells you to go find a pickaxe, Silksong expects you to break through it with your head.

The good

[] Movement is god-tier. Hornet glides through levels like a ballerina. Traversal is so fluid it's basically its own form of fun, so the huge map never feels like a chore to cross.
[] Combat has depth. Pogo, parries, deflecting projectiles, tools (spears, knives, potions, grenades), and Crests that completely change your moveset or healing.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 237176769

text:
Pogo, parries, deflecting projectiles, tools (spears, knives, potions, grenades), and Crests that completely change your moveset or healing. You can build a mage, a tool spammer, whatever you want.
[] Exploring new areas is the best part. Almost every biome brings new enemies, mechanics and upgrades. Greymoor, Shellwood, Deep Docks and the Citadel are phenomenal, classic Metroidvania design.
[] Art and music are stunning. Tons of tiny details, multilayered backgrounds, and another incredible Christopher Larkin soundtrack.

- Story and lore are coherent and well thought out, and Hornet actually talking makes the narrative much easier to follow.

The bad

[] Less Metroidvania, more Souls. Many areas are fairly linear with shortcuts. You clear them on the first pass and never come back. Backtracking often leads to a room with a handful of rosaries.
[] Some secrets are absurdly hidden, Dark Souls illusory wall style.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 237176769

text:
[] Some secrets are absurdly hidden, Dark Souls illusory wall style. Good luck getting 100% without a guide.
[] The balance feels like a stream challenge run. HK's endgame damage (2 masks per hit) becomes the default a few hours in, while your HP stays at base level. Getting knocked into spikes by a boss can take 4 masks in a second. The new healing (3 masks at once, but only with full silk) is the only thing that makes this work. If you get chunked with no silk, you need 9 hits on 1 HP to heal.
[] Stingy direct progression. Twice as many silk upgrades as HK for the same endpoint. Your first needle upgrade is basically it until Act 2. One extra mask barely matters when you die in 3 hits anyway.

text:
One extra mask barely matters when you die in 3 hits anyway.

[] Gauntlets everywhere. Locked-arena wave fights every 15 minutes against enemies you've already beaten, often copy-pasted arenas, often with no reward at all (drops disabled). One mandatory 10-wave gauntlet ends in a boss, so every death means 10 more minutes to try again.
[] Lazy bosses. Few of them, many with 2 to 4 attacks spammed at high speed and high damage. Lots of them spawn random adds, so RNG decides how hard the fight is.

Act 3 (spoilers)

Hollow Knight Silksong makes a couple giant swerves from its predecessor. The first is that this game is long, much longer than the first game, and the second is the game is far more combat focused. This creates a very different experience to Hollow Knight, that is extremely rewarding if you have the patience for it.

Equipment has taken a general nerf in the amount of combinations that you can do, but is offset by new moveset loadouts. This means the game is willing to let you play how you want, but it demands mastery of your given style. Bosses are incredibly well designed, most of them rely on a style of duck and weave combat in order to maintain high health while slowly whittling down health.

text:
TL;DR is that the game has more pros than cons, unless you aren't in for a challenge.

Silksong has beautiful artwork, fun fast-paced combat, and glorious music (Christopher Larkin you legend.) but its focus on dodging involves having a lot of bosses and enemies that have higher damage, when in the eyes of the first game, they shouldn't. A lot of the negative reviews probably come from players that have played the first game, like me, but are expecting this game to involve as much tanking hits as the first game did. The focus on Silksong is staying quick on your feet and trying to dodge as many hits as possible. But when you take the storyline, combat system, artwork, and music into account, I would say that it's best that you get it--as long as you're patient enough for the repeated boss attempts.

text:
Silksong is a great game, in terms of artwork, atmosphere, story, combat and general gameplay. It also happens to be very difficult, and you are constantly reminded of this fact. With that being said, if you are able to access a boss, you have the tools to deal with it, and you just need to learn its patterns and figure out a winning strategy.

Two of the biggest strengths of the game are movement and exploration. You can really fly around the map after a few unlocks, and your ability to rapidly change direction and positioning make combat feel incredibly dynamic and snappy. Every area also feels unique, and there are tonnes of secrets hidden away if you look hard enough.

text:
Original felt incredibly lonely and suffocating. Knight was exploring ruins of a once-great civilization, and trying to figure out what happened. Places you explore are destroyed, the music is sad and the NPCs are scarce.
Here, Hornet is trying to reach a specific place, meeting various named NPCs and pilgrims along the way. Pharloom feels lived in and lively, which is a surprising contrast to the first game. Surprising, but also fun.

The combat is also different. Rather than trying to replicate the precise, pixel-perfect combat from the first game, the devs leaned into Hornet's agility, and made the combat much more dynamic and acrobatic-like. Add to that well-telegraphed bosses with somewhat simple patterns and you have genuinely amazing combat that feels more like a dance with an enemy. text:
A Worthy Successor

After all these years of waiting, Silksong had an almost impossible task: live up to Hollow Knight.

And, for me, it succeeds.

Silksong takes everything that made the first game great and pushes it in a new direction. Hornet is faster, more agile, and much more dynamic than the Knight, which completely changes the way exploration and combat feel. Movement is incredibly fluid, and fighting enemies feels almost like a dance once you get used to it.

The World

Pharloom is absolutely beautiful.

Every area has its own identity, atmosphere, enemies, secrets, and soundtrack. There is always that feeling that something is hidden just around the corner, and exploration constantly rewards curiosity.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235193319

text:
There is always that feeling that something is hidden just around the corner, and exploration constantly rewards curiosity.

The world feels mysterious without simply copying Hollow Knight. It has its own personality, its own history, and plenty of things left unexplained for the player to discover.

Combat & Bosses

The combat is one of the biggest strengths of the game.

Hornet's speed and movement make fights much more aggressive and dynamic. The bosses are varied, memorable, and often require you to properly learn their patterns instead of simply attacking until one of you stops moving.

Personally, I didn't find the game particularly difficult. There were certainly challenging encounters, but the difficulty never felt excessive or unfair to me. Once I understood the patterns and adapted to the fights, most of them became very satisfying to overcome.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235193319

text:
Once I understood the patterns and adapted to the fights, most of them became very satisfying to overcome.

The Tools

This is probably my biggest criticism of the game.

The Tool system is a great idea in principle, but I don't think the game pushes the player enough to actually experiment with it.

You can create a loadout that works well in almost every situation and simply stick with it for a large portion of the game. Because of this, many of the Tools end up feeling more like optional alternatives rather than meaningful solutions to different problems.

I would have preferred the game to create more situations where a specific Tool, or a different combination of Tools, was genuinely useful or even necessary.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235193319

text:
I would have preferred the game to create more situations where a specific Tool, or a different combination of Tools, was genuinely useful or even necessary.

That would have encouraged experimentation and made changing your loadout feel like an important part of the gameplay rather than something you can mostly ignore once you've found a setup that works.

Music & Atmosphere

Christopher Larkin once again delivers an incredible soundtrack.

The music fits each area perfectly, from quiet and melancholic sections to intense boss fights. His work adds so much personality to Pharloom that the soundtrack often feels like an essential part of the world itself.

I personally saved quite a few tracks from the game, including Choral Chambers, Nyleth, and Bilewater. That probably says enough about how much I enjoyed the soundtrack.

Combined with the art direction, it creates an atmosphere that very few games can match.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235193319

text:
Combined with the art direction, it creates an atmosphere that very few games can match.

The Flaws

Apart from the Tool system, most of my criticisms are relatively minor.

There are moments where backtracking can become tedious, especially when trying to complete everything, and some objectives feel more like ways of extending the game than meaningful additions.

But these problems never outweighed the overall experience for me.

Final Thoughts

Silksong doesn't replace Hollow Knight, and it doesn't need to.

It takes the foundation of the original and builds something different around it. Hornet plays completely differently, Pharloom feels like its own world, and the exploration retains that same feeling of constantly discovering something new.

After such a ridiculously long wait, Team Cherry managed to do the hardest thing possible:

make a sequel that actually feels worth the wait.

9/10

Now I'm just waiting for Sea of Sorrow.

text:
The main attraction of hollow knight, and what I think the game did unbelievably exceptionally well, was the map. Not the mere pretty visuals of the biomes themselves, but specifically how well those biomes fitted toogether. You have a mountain, the highest point of the map. Below the mountain, you have a lake. Below the lake you have a city where its constantly raining because the lake is leaking through. Every single biome felt deliberately placed to make sense within the geography which is what made the world feel alive.

Silksong throws that ♥♥♥♥ out the window and just randomly places biomes haphazardly with no regard for how they actually fit in the world. You have a gigantic frozen mountain, that is somehow shorted than the citadel. Below the frozen ice mountain you have... a desert.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235511809

text:
Next to the citadel you have... the underground sewers. Yes. Not below the citadel, NEXT to the citadel you the UNDERGROUND SEWERS. The highest point of the right side of the map is literally an underground sewer. For reference, the highest point of the right side of the map in hollow knight was a mountain and the highest point on the left side was the edge of a gigantic cliff with the sky visible in the background.

So, the map is just random ♥♥♥♥ thrown toogether haphazardly. And the biomes themselves are not doing much legwork either. Even individual biomes in hollow knight felt like actual lived in places. The city of tears had the plaza in the middle and the towers to the sides, queen's station was a gigantic multi floor station with stagways on each side, deepnest was a complex network of untamed underground tunnels made by wild bugs.
title: Hollow Knight: Silksong — review 235511809

text:

text:
Best of Both Horrors

Over the years, my love for the Resident Evil series has only grown stronger, so I was incredibly excited for Requiem. Thankfully, the game did not disappoint. Requiem combines the horror, exploration, and level design of RE7 and RE8 with the action of RE4R, bringing together different eras of the series in a surprisingly well-balanced experience.

The best example of this is Leon and Grace. They aren't simply two characters we control at different points in the story; they represent two different sides of Resident Evil. Grace's sections are slower, more vulnerable, doesn't rely entirely on jumpscares; it uses atmosphere, sound design, and darkness to create tension.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 234802982

text:
Grace's sections are slower, more vulnerable, doesn't rely entirely on jumpscares; it uses atmosphere, sound design, and darkness to create tension. Resources are limited, and you often have to decide whether it's worth fighting or simply finding a way around a threat. The Blood Collector mechanic complements this approach nicely, adding another layer of resource management that fits Grace's vulnerable playstyle.

When you switch to Leon, the pace picks up considerably. His years of experience are reflected in his gameplay, allowing you to take on enemies more confidently and use your weapons much more aggressively. His sections are also more action-oriented, introducing semi-open areas that give you more freedom to explore, search for resources, and decide where you want to go next. I actually enjoyed this change of pace, although I don't think it always works perfectly.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 234802982

text:
I actually enjoyed this change of pace, although I don't think it always works perfectly. After the tightly controlled and tense sections with Grace, Leon's larger environments can sometimes make the game feel a little less focused. The tension naturally drops when you're given more space to explore, and some of the momentum from the more linear sections can be lost. Still, the contrast between the two characters does wonders for the pacing. After spending so much time feeling vulnerable as Grace, taking control of Leon feels genuinely satisfying. But once you start feeling too comfortable with Leon's strength, switching back to Grace immediately reminds you how fragile you actually are.

The level design also captures the classic Resident Evil feeling well. Interconnected areas, locked doors, backtracking, hidden rooms, and plenty of reasons to explore make the world feel rewarding to navigate.

Interconnected areas, locked doors, backtracking, hidden rooms, and plenty of reasons to explore make the world feel rewarding to navigate. I also enjoyed the puzzles. They aren't particularly difficult. In fact, I could even call some of them subpar but they're still enjoyable. Finding an item, figuring out where to use it, returning to a previously visited area, and eventually unlocking a new path recreates that classic Resident Evil gameplay loop perfectly.

Leon and Grace also complement each other well narratively. Leon has spent years experiencing the horrors of this world and knows how to deal with them, while Grace approaches them from a much more vulnerable and unfamiliar perspective. Leon represents the history and experience of the series, while Grace gives us a fresher way of experiencing its world.

Ghosts of Raccoon City: A Stunning 30th Anniversary Celebration

Resident Evil Requiem had the monumental task of celebrating the franchise’s 30th anniversary while simultaneously pushing it forward. By splitting its campaign between two distinct protagonists with entirely different gameplay styles, Capcom has delivered a masterclass that perfectly balances the suffocating dread of the series' roots with its legendary, pulse-pounding action.

A Stunning Return to Raccoon City
Decades after the iconic missile strike, returning to the overgrown, haunted ruins of Raccoon City is a surreal experience. The derelict Wrenwood Hotel serves as the game's primary epicenter, and it is a masterpiece of environmental design. Powered by the RE Engine, the game’s lighting and photorealistic textures are staggering.

The engine continues its legacy of fantastic optimization, maintaining smooth, high framerates whether you are cranking settings on an RTX 4070 desktop or playing natively on a Steam Deck OLED.

Grace Ashcroft: Pure Survival Horror
The heart of Requiem's terror lies with its new protagonist, FBI intelligence analyst Grace Ashcroft. Unlike the highly trained combat specialists the series is known for, Grace introduces a desperate new layer of vulnerability. text:
That's the state of PC gaming now and Requiem is no exception, but once it's dialled in, it's a genuinely beautiful game to sit in.

The structure is what makes it for me. The first half alternates between Grace Ashcroft and Leon Kennedy, and that alternation is brilliant. You mostly control Grace, and she's the opposite of the usual Resident Evil protagonist: she's an FBI technical analyst with barely any field experience, she's nervous, she's out of her depth, and the game makes you feel every bit of that. Playing on the standard difficulty, without unlimited saves, those sections are unbelievably tense. You're rationing everything, planning your routes, deciding which enemies are worth fighting and which ones you simply run from. It's proper survival horror in the lineage of RE7 and the RE2 remake, and it had me genuinely anxious in a way the series hasn't managed in a while.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 235750161

text:
Then you get these short bursts with Leon, a few minutes at a time, packed with action. As pacing, it's perfect. Just as the tension with Grace is about to become exhausting, you're handed the fantasy of being the veteran who actually knows what he's doing, and then it's snatched away and you're back to being scared. That contrast is the smartest thing the game does.

Where I was a little more disappointed is the second half, where you're playing Leon and only Leon, and it turns into a full action game. Don't get me wrong, it's still good, and the locations are fantastic. Revisiting places tied to the series' history, with Grace's connection to her mother Alyssa and the Raccoon City survivors running underneath it, is exactly the kind of fan service I want.

But sustained action just isn't what I wanted from a game that had spent ten hours proving how good it was at making me afraid. The tension deflates. The story I have nothing bad to say about. It's well constructed, it's told with restraint rather than burying you in exposition, and it ties Grace's personal investigation into the wider series history without feeling like a nostalgia exercise. text: Resident Evil Requiem is a culmination of all Capcom has learned and innovated over the course of this long-running series of games. Both long-term fans and newcomers to the series are bound to find things to enjoy in this game. From the slow-paced, survival horror-flavoured gameplay in Grace's sections, where one must engage in inventory management and selective combat with enemies, to the faster, flashier, often cinematic, action horror-flavoured romps in Leon's sections, Requiem aims to deliver a unique compress-and-release-style experience not found in many other mainstream horror games, by periodically alternating between the two protagonists. And it does so successfully to a large extent.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 236007881

text:
And it does so successfully to a large extent.

Mechanically, the gameplay is as solid as it gets for AAA games, and is balanced around the two protagonists' level of experience. The sound design gets top marks: from the pop of firing the Requiem revolver to the shrieks and thumping footsteps of the stalker enemy in Grace's parts, this is one of those games that MUST be played with a good set of headphones to experience it to its fullest extent. The graphical quality is outstanding, and players with high-end hardware are in for a treat. Heck, even mid or lower tier rigs can get decent performance from this game, a testament to Capcom's ability in optimising games built using their in-house RE Engine (apart from a few notable hiccups in recent years).
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 236007881

text:
There are, however, a few points of criticism. For a full-priced AAA game, Requiem is somewhat short, though this criticism is somewhat mitigated by the game being quite replay-friendly. Regardless, I would argue this game is maybe not as replayable as the remakes of RE4 or RE2. Particularly, Requiem has a few unskippable walking sections, where the player simply needs to move forward. Allowing players to simply skip past these sections after the first playthrough would be a welcome change.

Next, as with most Resident Evil games, the earlier sections overshadow the later ones in terms of quality and memorability. The care centre and its basement, which all happen before the halfway point of the game, are the best parts.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 236007881

text:
Also, the story is somewhat silly, and sometimes even ridiculous, compared to other Resident Evil games, where the entire plot revolves around biological weapons and mass destruction. While the graphical quality is great, the art design falls somewhat flat. From around the halfway point of the game, the design switches from the rich, homely, yet eerie feel of the care centre, to drab grey-and-white colour palettes. All these were not really issues for me, but might be useful for others who value story, length, art design, and consistency of gameplay quality.

Lastly, the post-launch updates for this game seem to have stopped with Leon Must Die Forever for now, with no official updates for the release of the story DLC for this game, announced several months ago at the time of writing; this could change in the future.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 236007881

text:
Also, Leon Must Die Forever, a roguelike-styled add-on, is somewhat mid. Though you do get it for the low, low price of free, so there's that.

Overall, a very solid 9/10, maybe even a 9.5/10 if/when the story DLC drops. Highly recommend getting this, even at full price. Though maybe hold out for a sale, since Resident Evil games seem to be discounted every other month.

An excellent effort to honor the 30th anniversary of R.E.

Jun Takeuchi's & Koshi Nakanishi's vision since 2014 which ultimately saved the decaying Resident Evil franchise since Resident Evil 7, has shown no signs of slowing down. Requiem has become the fastest selling Resident Evil title of all time to date, releasing close to the franchise's anniversary date, and ultimately honoring the series as whole in Requiem.

Requiem is an absolute powerhouse, blending the scope of tying in two different perspectives from previous titles, immersing the individual into two different playing styles. This is blended perfectly by its pacing, where the stress and tension builds up to a high peak with Grace, and then changes over to a more action focused pace with Leon.

Playing as Grace, you'll be forced into stressful and suffocating close quarters, relying on critical thinking skills to solve puzzles, ration provisions, and addressing the threats of monsters imposing on oneself. Grace's playthrough is reminiscent of the franchise's core feels of a sense of dread and suffocation, where costly mistakes are punishing, jump scares are brutal, and the overwhelming psychological effects leave a lasting effect on the player.

text:
(Warning: This review contains heavy narrative and boss-fight spoilers.)

Resident Evil: Requiem successfully balances two completely different mechanical tones without breaking the core experience. It is a fantastic game that succeeds as a proper successor to Resident Evil 4, keeping you highly engaged mechanically. However, while the gameplay shines, the pacing and narrative structure completely collapse in the middle act.

THE HIGHS (Atmosphere, Mechanics & Payoff):

Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Center: A legitimately perfect starting area. Capcom tried the hospital environment in the RE3 Remake and it was just okay, but this iteration is phenomenal.

The Axe: Leon’s combat feels distinctly different from the RE4 Remake. Replacing the tactical knife with the axe is an incredibly satisfying mechanical shift that gives his melee loop a heavy, brutal weight.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 237329020

text:
Replacing the tactical knife with the axe is an incredibly satisfying mechanical shift that gives his melee loop a heavy, brutal weight.

The Emotional Conclusion: Grace’s arc is handled beautifully. After surviving an incredibly isolating and terrifying campaign, the fact that she actually saves and adopts Emily is an adorable, well-earned victory that perfectly anchors her side of the nightmare.

THE LOWS (The Pacing Collapse & Narrative Flaws):

The Raccoon City Narrative Halt: The atmosphere here is masterful—seeing a city permanently trapped in 1998 gives off eerie, The Last of Us vibes. But the narrative comes to a screeching halt. You are stuck in this city for what feels like forever, and Victor Gideon and Zeno just vanish off-screen for 1-2 hours. You get absolutely zero plot development until you finally reach the RPD.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 237329020

text:
You get absolutely zero plot development until you finally reach the RPD.

Nostalgia Over Narrative: To mask the dead pacing in Raccoon City, the game throws in boss fights against Mr. X and HUNK. While mechanically fun, they are entirely unnecessary to the story. Mr. X adds literally nothing to the plot, and the HUNK encounter ends way too quickly.

Sidelining the Protagonist: The game clearly wants to show how important Grace Ashcroft is, but it completely sacrifices its own narrative to do so. After she kills the girl, Grace just disappears. She is effectively sidelined until the final quarter of the game, reduced to nothing more than a walking macguffin.

The Villain Vacuum: Do not let the marketing fool you—Victor Gideon is not an active antagonist.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 237329020

text:
He is the most interesting villain Capcom has written in a long time, but Leon just takes him out and he disappears. Meanwhile, Zeno is essentially a weaker Albert Wesker clone, and because the script abandons him for hours, we have absolutely no idea who he is.

A Generic Arsenal: For a franchise known for its weapon variety, the firearms here are extremely generic (Pistol, Shotgun, Sniper, SMG, and the "Requiem" Magnum). It desperately needed more experimental or unique firearms.

The Difficulty Curve: Playing on Standard, the game felt noticeably too easy through the mid-to-late sections.

Exhausting Lore Retcons: Capcom has retconned who orchestrated the Raccoon City incident again. First it was the US Government, then RE6 blamed Derek C. Simmons, and now it was the faction protecting Elips. Capcom desperately needs to stick to their established lore.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 237329020

text:
Capcom desperately needs to stick to their established lore.

It is a massive success mechanically that expertly juggles two distinct gameplay styles, but it undeniably sacrifices its narrative momentum for nostalgia. The combat and environments are easily worth your time, but Capcom absolutely must land the story in the upcoming DLC to forgive the base game's structural shortcomings.

text:
Resident Evil Requiem

I played RE: Requiem for over 28 hours and absolutely loved it. It's not the best game in the series in my opinion, but it's definitely top 5, if not top 3 for me.

The Gameplay

It takes a lot of what I liked about RE4 and RE7 and blends it together really nicely. You get the action and faster-paced gameplay that I loved from RE4, while still getting a lot of the tension, atmosphere, and horror that made RE7 so good.

One of my favorite things about the game is the shifting playstyles. Having the game switch things up between characters and gameplay styles keeps things from getting stale, and I never really felt like I was doing the exact same thing for too long.

text:
Even when I was playing through areas a second time, there were enough differences in how I approached them that it still felt fun.

There are definitely moments where it feels like a classic Resident Evil horror game, but then it can turn around and throw you into a much more action-heavy section. Normally that kind of back-and-forth could feel jarring, but I think Requiem pulls it off surprisingly well.

It feels like Capcom took lessons from several different games in the series and figured out how to make them work together instead of just picking one direction and sticking with it.

text:

For Me, the Best Resident Evil Yet

Resident Evil 7 was the game that got me into the series, but Requiem is the first entry that has actually replaced it as my favorite.

---

[/hr]

A Great Mix of Horror and Action

What makes Resident Evil Requiem work so well for me is the balance between its two different styles.

The Grace sections focus much more on sneaking, tension, and horror. You feel more vulnerable, you never fully know what is waiting for you, and there are some genuinely good scares.

The Leon sections go in the opposite direction with more action, more weapons, and a much faster pace. That contrast works extremely well and keeps the game feeling fresh from start to finish.
title: Resident Evil Requiem — review 236270284

text:
That contrast works extremely well and keeps the game feeling fresh from start to finish.

---

[/hr]

Story, Atmosphere, and Gameplay

The story is focused and consistently engaging. It has that typical Resident Evil feeling where you always want to keep going just a little longer because you need to know what happens next.

The atmosphere is excellent, the music is strong, the enemies work well, and the weapons are simply fun to use.

Exploration also feels well balanced. There is enough backtracking and searching to keep that classic Resident Evil feeling without making it tedious.

The pacing and overall length felt right to me as well. Nothing dragged on for too long, and the game kept moving at a good pace throughout.

Technical Performance and Replay Value

If another massive game had not entered the conversation this year, Resident Evil Requiem would easily be my personal Game of the Year.

text:
And then there is the other thing. The combat. The game's core concept is to incorporate mechanically-demanding dodge-parry mechanics into a turn-based combat system. I've seen the idea work in a few other games. But here, it's actually really awful. The game is desperately trying to be a soulslike JPRPG, but I'm sorry--there's nothing fun about a soulslike where your feet are nailed to the ground and you're constantly flipping through menus. Nor do I care for a JRPG where strategy comes secondary to raw mechanical input.

Parry counterattacks are implemented in such a way that, while they are pretty obnoxious to pull off (the visual indicators are so inconsistent that it's sometimes easier to parry if you don't look at your screen at all, and rely exclusively on audio queues) but they're also overbalanced as hell.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 234825746

text:
If you don't parry, you die. And if you do parry, you take no damage, you deal massive damage, and you recharge your resources. It's so strong that every other combat mechanic in the game becomes irrelevant--you can skip all your turns, only parry, and still win the majority of battles. And frankly most of the combat encounters don't have interesting mechanics to them at all, other than increasingly ridiculous (I've heard up to 20 consecutive parries in late-game) parry combos, and parrying increasingly weird, gimmicky fakeouts.

Learning to consistently land parries in the first few hours of gameplay was fun, and was satisfying for a few more hours after that but halfway through the first act it had already become boring.

text:
Phenomenal. Everything I love about games, media, and art in general. Clearly made with a singular, creative, vision with the goal being to create a wonderful game and nothing else.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 knows how to make an entrance. Its opening is beautiful, uncomfortable and quietly devastating, establishing a world where everyone lives with an expiration date. That premise could easily have carried a straightforward adventure about stopping a mysterious enemy. Thankfully, the game has far more on its mind.

The story is its strongest point. Beneath the expedition and the unanswered questions lies a deeply personal story about loss and belonging. What do you do with grief when there is nowhere to put it? How much of yourself becomes tied to the people you love? These questions give the journey weight without turning every conversation into a philosophical speech. text:
I have some a few nitpicks, but these don't bring it down from being a 10.

The Positives:

This is (near) perfect turn-based combat. The developers took systems from almost every RPG and put them together perfectly, and it all comes down to one very good decision on the developers part: AP. In most RPGs you have mana, a resource that starts full after being healed but goes down the more you use it for spells and ♥♥♥♥. In Clair Obscur its the opposite: your AP starts low, and you have to do actions to build it. Thankfully you have so many different ways to build AP across characters, and very unique ways to use it throughout the entire game.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235743699

text: Thankfully you have so many different ways to build AP across characters, and very unique ways to use it throughout the entire game. As for defense, you have the universal options of dodging (which has a longer invulnerability window and less recovery time) or parrying (which has a tighter window, can't be spammed as easily, but rewards you with 1 AP per parry AND if you parry all hits of a sequence you get a counterattack). I could go on forever about the other parts of combat, but I think it's better for the player to experience it firsthand. You always feel like you have something to do in battles, and I don't think I've ever run from a battle out of boredom.

text:
The (very few) Negatives:

For an RPG that's clearly well-versed in the all time greats (Thousand Year Door, Chrono Trigger, Persona 5) and goes out of its way to use its combat systems to the fullest, there are some headscratching choices they made here and there.

The one big flaw in the combat system is that you can't switch party members mid fight. You get to use your reserve members if the first wave get KO'd, but you can't actively swap them out like a lot of turn based RPGs. This matters particularly if your character is using a certain element type on their weapon, and the enemy is immune to that type entirely. At best it makes a fight more obnoxious than it should be, and at worst it forces you to abandon and go back to the nearest save point to reformat your party.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235743699

text:
The second big issue is that if you retry a fight and it has a cutscene before it... it reloads the cutscene and you gotta skip it all over again. Maybe the cutscenes mask loading the fight? But I doubt it given how fast it goes into it when you skip the cutscene.

Some other minor nitpicks. There's no minimap whatsoever. There's an overworld map, that is a good map imo, but no dungeon maps. I think for the most part... this is fine. The dungeons have a lot of different side paths, but they're designed in a way that you don't really get lost most of the time. There's a few places I definitely would've preferred a minimap though, so I wish that had been a togglable option.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235743699

text:
There's a few places I definitely would've preferred a minimap though, so I wish that had been a togglable option.

Lastly, I've heard some reviewers mention that doing side content first makes main story fights very easy. I didn't feel like this was the case, but I was also playing on the hardest difficulty. I honestly feel like the hardest difficulty should be the go-to for playing the game, as it really challenges you to optimize your offense and defense. There is a 9,999 damage cap for much of the game, and this does keep you from beating some side bosses in the middle of the game. I wonder if the lower difficulty options allowed the reviewers to beat bosses they really shouldn't have and given them a drastic amount of levels.

Anyways, 10/10 game. Deserved every award it got.

There is something called a “Gommage” where everyone who is of age or older are “Thanos snapped” out of existence. So the people who are going to disappear during the next Gommage set out on an expedition to try to put an end to all the death.
When arriving at the expedition landing point, it’s like you’re walking across decades of lore and the result of failed attempts that push only slightly further to make way for the next expedition. It’s grim, it’s dark, and yet hauntingly beautiful.
I was immersed right from the get-go and while the plot didn’t end as strong as it started, it kept me interested throughout.

Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [9/10]

The general gameplay loop consists of going to a designated area, fighting your way through enemies via turn-based battles, and eventually ending on a boss fight with long cutscenes sprinkled in between.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235154542

text:
This being a turned-based RPG truly sets the bar for the potential of turn-based games. The combat flawlessly weaves in dodges and parries into the combat that turns the combat into a fast-paced and insanely engaging difference from other turn-based games like Final Fantasy.
The game's progression system is interesting in that it’s deceptively simple, yet opens up as the game advances. Instead of a large amount of gear, you get a weapon and 3 “Picto” slots, which are basically accessory slots that give passive abilities. The catch is that you can unlock those Picto abilities to equip on any character by using points they get when leveling up.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235154542

text:
The catch is that you can unlock those Picto abilities to equip on any character by using points they get when leveling up. It reminds me of Final Fantasy 9 how you use a piece of gear in enough battles and you can unlock the passive abilities to equip without the gear (just on any character here). The equipped Pictos combined with the weapon passive combined with character skills, of which you can have 6, allows some fairly intricate build potential, especially as you progress in the game and unlock some crazier abilities.

The difficulty is good. I played on Normal difficulty and was challenged, but rarely died. The game is exceptionally forgiving in allowing you to redo fights or just simply backout of fights. The game uses a lot of Dark Souls mechanics though dodges and parrying, but doesn’t actively punish you for failing, which is great for experimentation.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235154542

text:
The game uses a lot of Dark Souls mechanics though dodges and parrying, but doesn’t actively punish you for failing, which is great for experimentation.
However, there are optional bosses, and unless you are either insanely overleveled/optimized or a god at parrying/dodging, you’re going to constantly get 1 or 2-shot. The optional content is no joke (look up the Simon fight on Youtube).

Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [10/10]

The graphics are exceptionally good. This is easily PS5-era fidelity and beyond. The cutscenes look stellar and the area's art style is phenomenal.
The performance was perfect. I played the game fully maxed and ran into no issues at all.
Perhaps the only thing I can nitpick here is with the Unreal Engine making animations and movements stiff, floaty, and often going through the environment.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235154542

text:
This is a consistent thing with 3rd person UE games and it’s still noticeable here, despite the otherwise beautiful looking setting.
I did encounter a bug that seemed to have a lot of discussion online - audio crackling during combat, which is a shame because the music is SO good. I wasn’t able to find a fix for this, despite all my other games sounding fine.

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD

Audio – [10/10]

I absolutely cannot stress enough how amazing the music is in this game. Simple random encounter fights have musical scores that rival end boss fights in other JRPGs. The soundtrack is so good, that I literally added multiple songs to my Spotify playlist.
Aside from the amazing soundtrack, the voice acting is very good, a slight complaint being how there are 4x “Rough & sandpaper” voice sounding male characters. The men badly need some diversity.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235154542

text:
The men badly need some diversity.

Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10]

There is a NG+, but due to lack of player choice and a mostly linear game, there isn’t a whole lot of replay value.
There is a lot of optional content to do and level up, but as far as having a different experience or outcome when replaying the game, it’s not really possible outside of builds, which don’t open up fully until the endgame anyways.

Final Verdict – [9/10]

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (COE33) has fully earned the award of Game of the Year 2025. I was constantly impressed, over and over again, as I played through the game. It’s truly an experience. The hardest part for me is to decide whether to rate this game a 9 or a 10.

Once I hit Act 3 and the big reveal presented itself, I was a bit letdown after learning that the entire world that the expedition takes place in isn’t really real. It’s a fairly old narrative deflection and kind of made all the amazing lore in the beginning not as meaningful. But still, at that point I’m 40 hours in and no way I’m stopping.

text:
The good? SO much. The game is simply phenomenal. The narrative starts out so strong that it's hard to put down. There are so many mysteries and questions that I have to know, it’s like reading a good book.
The music is astounding. I can’t get numerous songs out of my head and they are on my Spotify list now.
I think more than anything is that E33 shows the potential that turn-based RPGs still have. While games like Final Fantasy have moved into more action-oriented combat, E33 has taken the classic turn-based formula and just smacked on the Dark Souls mechanics to turn it into some of the most exciting combat I’ve ever played. It’s truly game changing and I hope more games follow the blueprints laid here to inject new elements into old systems.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was an interesting experience to finish, but after completing the game, I can’t say I would recommend buying it at full price. Maybe for a few dollars or euros on a deep sale, but there are simply too many much better-developed RPGs and JRPGs available.

text:
I kept expecting the narrative to introduce something that would significantly change my perception of what was happening, but that never really happened. I also found some of the conflicts and contradictions in the characters’ motivations more off-putting than compelling. Instead of making them feel more complex or human, these moments often made their actions and decisions harder for me to connect with. Character development in general felt limited, which was particularly disappointing for a game that places so much emphasis on its narrative and cast.

The gameplay is enjoyable at first, but as an RPG it lacks depth. Most of the systems are straightforward, and there isn’t much need to carefully think about your build or experiment with different approaches.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235699901

text:
Once you understand the basic mechanics, the effective choices become fairly obvious. Build variety also feels quite limited for the genre. I would have liked to see more meaningful trade-offs, stronger specialization, and more viable ways to build and play each character.

The world itself is good. I liked the overall art direction, environment design, monster design, and character design. Visually, the game has a distinctive identity and there are plenty of locations that are enjoyable to explore. The presentation is clearly one of the game’s stronger aspects.

Overall, I finished the game, but I wouldn’t recommend buying it at anything close to full price. Perhaps it’s worth picking up for a few euros during a deep sale. There are many RPGs and JRPGs on the market with deeper gameplay systems, more interesting build variety, stronger character development, and more engaging stories.

text:
I start Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 knowing one thing:
this world is already counting my days.

Every year, the Paintress wakes up, writes a number, and everyone older than that number simply disappears.
No boss fight.
No last words.
Just erased — politely, artistically, and brutally.

You don’t play as a chosen one.
You play as someone already scheduled to die.
Expedition 33 isn’t about saving the world — it’s about walking forward anyway, fully aware that time is winning.

The combat is turn-based, but it refuses to feel safe.
Timing matters.
Dodging matters.
Every action feels like the game asking, “Are you sure this is how you want to spend this moment?”
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 235194282

text:
Every action feels like the game asking, “Are you sure this is how you want to spend this moment?”

The world is haunting.
Beautiful in a way that hurts.
Surreal cities, broken landscapes, and silence that feels heavier than dialogue.
Even when nothing attacks you, the atmosphere does.

And the characters…
They don’t speak like heroes.
They speak like people who know the ending and still choose to move.
There’s hope here — but it’s quiet, fragile, and constantly under threat.

• Joined the expedition → Accepted my expiration date.
• Fought beautifully → Still felt small.
• Kept moving forward → Because stopping doesn’t change the number.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is art + inevitability + quiet defiance.
If you love this game… congratulations, you’re comfortable staring mortality in the face and pressing “continue.”

9.5/10 – Came for the art.
Stayed because the countdown never stops, and neither did I.

Almost as good as the hype says - and that’s still pretty damn good.

While my expectations were met in that regard, I have to say overall the game is still fantastic. Since it has been glazed so much, I mostly want to break down both what makes it so special and the issues that I rarely see anyone talking about.

What Makes the Game Phenomenal

text:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is the kind of game that reminds you why you fell in love with RPGs in the first place. Sandfall Interactive delivers an ambitious, emotionally devastating adventure that blends classic turn based structure with modern action sensibilities, and the result is something truly special.

The premise alone is gripping. Every year, the Paintress wakes and paints a number on her monolith, and everyone of that age turns to smoke and fades away. Expedition 33 is humanity's latest attempt to end the cycle, and the weight of that mission hangs over every conversation, camp scene, and battle. This is a story about grief, sacrifice, and finding meaning in borrowed time, and it never flinches from the hard questions.
title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — review 237140171

text:
Combat is a standout. Turn based fundamentals are enhanced with real time dodging, parrying, and counterattacking, keeping you engaged on every enemy turn instead of waiting your way through them. Mastering the timing of a perfect parry is endlessly satisfying, and the deep build system, with its pictos, luminas, and varied character kits, gives you plenty of room to experiment.

Visually and musically, it's breathtaking. The Belle Époque inspired world is rendered with striking artistry, full of surreal landscapes and unforgettable character designs. Lorien Testard's score is haunting and gorgeous, lifting key story moments into something you'll remember long after the credits roll.

The cast is the heart of it all. Gustave, Maelle, Lune, Sciel, Verso, and Monoco feel like real people with real flaws, and the writing and voice acting make every bond feel earned.

text:
The biggest problem with Wilds is that it removes almost all friction and with it, a lot of what made Monster Hunter feel like Monster Hunter.

Almost every mechanic that used to require preparation, decision-making or knowledge has been streamlined away.

You barely walk anymore. Seikret handles most of the traveling, lets you heal and sharpen on the move, and even gets you back on your feet after taking a hit. Items don't need to be picked up anymore, just shoot them with the Slinger. Monster drops teleport straight into your inventory.

Resources are basically infinite. Money, points, consumables and materials never feel scarce. There is almost no grinding. Most monsters only need to be hunted a few times to get everything you want, and even decorations and Artian gear are extremely easy to obtain.
title: Monster Hunter Wilds — review 235680283

text:
Most monsters only need to be hunted a few times to get everything you want, and even decorations and Artian gear are extremely easy to obtain.

The Palico handles healing and status recovery for you, capture thresholds are practically impossible to miss, and mechanics like tremors, wind pressure, blights and especially stun barely matter anymore. You can cook and restock whenever you want, even during a hunt. Fainting barely has any consequences because you keep your food buffs.

And then there is the actual combat.

There is almost no challenge. Monsters spend huge amounts of time knocked down or locked into wound-break animations. You don't really have to learn their moves or earn openings anymore, just attack wounds and the monster falls over. Triple-carting feels almost impossible because the monster will often die before it can seriously threaten you.
title: Monster Hunter Wilds — review 235680283

text:
Triple-carting feels almost impossible because the monster will often die before it can seriously threaten you.

The result is that you don't really need to learn the maps, prepare for hunts, manage resources, understand monster behavior or grind for gear. You just fight the monster, collect everything automatically and move on.

And that's the biggest disappointment for me.

Wilds is polished, beautiful and fun, but it has streamlined so much of Monster Hunter that it removed a lot of the reason I loved the series in the first place.

Monster Hunter: Wild- Oh boy, this is going to be a long one. I love this franchise and want to bring the right people in and share my thoughts on how it could improve. I will make this review as thorough as possible, so let us get into it.

CHAPTER 1: The Story
______________________________
Unlike all other Monster Hunter games I have played, this game takes a much more traditional approach to its storytelling. Instead of having brief story moments tied to key quests unlocked after a long phase of grinding, or having the narrative run through the entirety of LR and HR, this game instead puts the story front and center.

On the other hand, story has never been a focus of MonHun games for a good reason.

CHAPTER 2: High Rank

Monster Hunter Wilds is an absolute triumph of creature design, visceral combat, and sprawling, living ecosystems. The sheer scale of the new biomes and the fluidity of the weapon movesets make every hunt an unforgettable spectacle.

However, the game suffers from severe performance issues that heavily impact the experience. On many systems, frame rate stutters, optimization hiccups, and muddy texture streaming drag down the immersion, making smooth gameplay a constant battle against the hardware.

text:
Abstract
I like Monster Hunter Wilds a lot, even with its numerous flaws, and I believe that it will only get even better once Ascendance releases in 2027. Most of my enjoyment comes from set building and assisting others in difficult endgame hunts.
However, I won’t deny that this is very divisive entry to the series, and your enjoyment may differ significantly from mine even if you are a Monster Hunter fan.

Positives

- Endgame set building is very open-ended and allows for a lot of player creativity if you’re willing to go off-meta. I can stack on 3-4 different set skill bonuses and I love it.
title: Monster Hunter Wilds — review 235436387

text:
- The monster roster is diverse and there is a good selection of 9-10 star monsters that you can grind out in the endgame. I’m enjoying the fight variety more compared to the base game of “Wyvern Hunter” World.

- Probably my favorite High Rank out of any of the base game Monster Hunter that I’ve played thus far.

Neutral

- Focus mode. I like it well enough, but some people really don’t like how it massively changes the feel of combat. Some might argue that it tips the scale too much into the player’s favor, trivializing a lot of fights.

- How some of the weapons feel and play in Wilds has changed significantly as well. My mains, SnS and Lance, feel good and got nice moveset updates. But I don’t enjoy using certain weapons like Hammer, Greatsword, and Charge Blade anymore. YMMV
title: Monster Hunter Wilds — review 235436387

text:
Negatives

- The difficulty curve is stupid. Low Rank and early High Rank do not transition well into lategame High Rank at all. It goes from being a bit on the easier side to completely walloping you without mercy. A lot of SOS players (both host and joining) are just not prepared to deal with the Arch-Tempereds and other 9-10 star freaks waiting for them at the end of High Rank.

- The main story itself was fine, but I didn't like how many walking sections there were and how on-rails it was. Luckily the main story is like 5-ish hours long IIRC, and you have a lot more freedom in High Rank.

text: Update 9/17/2026 - After trying basically everything, I found a recommendation from game launch to limit the wattage in AMD Adrenalin for AMD GPUs because for some reason this game can cause it to spike wattage massively and then it 'ejects' the device, presumably to protect the card. Turns out, that's what was leading to my D3D DEVICE_REMOVED error. Instead of downpatching drivers as most current guides suggest, I updated to the latest version of everything, leave Adrenalin running (instead of disabling it, again as most current troubleshooting suggests), and put a -20% limit on my 9070 XT's wattage. Runs fine now.

Game is really fun and now playable, so updating to recommended and leaving this advice in case it helps any of you.

text:
I'll recommend this game because if you're considering it, you've likely played Hades first, and if you liked that, you'll probably enjoy the sequel too.

Differences between Hades and Hades II
The game has the same core mechanics as the first one, with a few key differences. Some features are completely new, like having familiars (pets) for bonuses and gathering materials to craft upgrades or garden. Others are just aesthetic changes that serve the same purpose, like upgrading your stats through Arcana Cards instead of the Mirror of Night.

The biggest difference is that there are two distinct paths you can take each night: you can go up to the surface or down into the Underworld. You're needed in both places, as the conflict is unfolding on Olympus and in Tartarus at the same time.

text:

However, there's a different learning curve for each path, and sometimes you're doing suicide runs to the surface (which is kinda harder) just to fetch some garlic or whatever before you can keep making progress down below, which can feel like a waste of time.

This sequel might be targeting the girlies, as it has a lot of cute pets, a gardening mechanic, a female MC with a lot of feelings, a witchy theme, singing sessions with Artemis, and all sorts of cute cozy elements that a lot of them will love.

Hades II is one of those games that makes me deeply suspicious of the concept of a “sequel.” Usually, when a game is as beloved as Hades, following it up presents a simple problem: how on earth do you improve upon something that already feels damn near perfected? text: It is a remarkably ambitious expansion of the entire formula, introducing new characters, environments, combat systems, routes, mechanics, and enough mythology to make keeping track of who is related to whom feel like a second gameplay mechanic. XD Hades II follows Melinoë, the younger sister of Zagreus, as she attempts to overthrow Chronos, the Titan of Time who has seized control of the Underworld. Rather than retracing Zagreus’ escape attempt, Melinoë repeatedly breaks into the Underworld, fighting toward Chronos. And somehow, Supergiant has made that premise feel natural. Well, mostly natural. This is still Hades II, after all, so naturally there is also a King Vermin named Uh-Oh who is apparently hellbent on exacting revenge for whatever Zagreus did to his ancestors in the first game. text: And then there is Melinoë herself. Where Zagreus felt like a fast, aggressive warrior constantly improvising through danger, Melinoë feels much more deliberate. Her combat revolves around positioning, magical control and Magick, with her Cast creating a binding area that can hold enemies in place. Suddenly, you aren't merely asking, “What can I hit?” You are asking, “Where do I want everything to be when I hit it?” Which is a surprisingly sophisticated question for someone who is about to turn a room full of monsters into artistic paste. XD Her Omega attacks push this further. Holding an attack or ability allows Melinoë to channel a more powerful version, consuming Magick for enhanced effects. Of course, accidentally holding the wrong button and spending all your Magick on one humble enemy means experiencing the ancient Greek tragedy known as “skill issue.” Very prominent in Homer's books I can concur lol.

The weapons give Melinoë distinct playstyles, while their alternate aspects ensure they are not simply interchangeable stat sticks. Some encourage close-range aggression, others reward distance and positioning, while others turn the battlefield into a particularly violent mathematics equation. And then Boons enter the equation. text: The greatest expansion, however, comes from the world itself. Hades II gives Melinoë multiple destinations, including the Surface, creating a much broader structure for each run. Instead of a single linear descent, your journey can branch into radically different environments, enemies and challenges. The Underworld still possesses that familiar Hades identity, but the Surface introduces an entirely different atmosphere. Ephyra feels alive in contrast with the Underworld's enclosed environments, while later regions escalate the visual and mechanical spectacle further. The Surface especially feels like Supergiant asking, “What if we took everything you learned underground and then made you do it somewhere much less comfortable?” Apparently the answer is fire. Lots of fire. And enemies who would very much like you to experience all of it personally and generously enough, free of charge! XD

text:
Seeing their next game be a sequel to their most recent - and most successful - outing, it seemed like my goats had fallen for the bag.

I was happily proven wrong. Hades 2 is more than worthy as a successor, improving on the original in (almost) every single way. It is the most polished, most refined version of what Supergiant has proven themselves masters of. The broadest cast of well written, well performed, wonderfully drawn characters, who - despite their apparent divinity - are deeply human and relevant in struggle and tone.

text: Night City is a colossal purgatory forged from steel and blood, a place where towering skyscrapers strangle the sun and neon light bleeds into the asphalt. This city never truly gives you a choice in how to live; it simply waits for you to decide how you will die. The cursed bullet we took to the head in that desolate landfill, thanks to Dexter DeShawn's betrayal, the very bullet Misty turned into a necklace, is not merely the beginning of the game. It is a ticking bomb hanging against our chest, the fatal price of our arrogance and our desperate hunger to become a legend. Every second that cold metal touches our skin, it whispers that we are slowly fading away.
title: Cyberpunk 2077 — review 234898791

text:
Every second that cold metal touches our skin, it whispers that we are slowly fading away.

The neon-drenched summits of Night City promise to carve your name into history in letters of gold, to make you an immortal legend. And at first, we believed that captivating lie. That is, until we lost Jackie, bleeding out in our arms in the back of that bloodstained Delamain cab. Jackie wanted to become a legend in Night City. He wanted his name to be remembered, to become someone who truly mattered. But as his blood slipped through our fingers, something inside V began to change for the very first time. In that backseat, V realizes that the pursuit of becoming a legend can actually mean burying the people you love with your own hands.
title: Cyberpunk 2077 — review 234898791

text:
In that backseat, V realizes that the pursuit of becoming a legend can actually mean burying the people you love with your own hands. The devastating loss of Jackie, followed by betrayal and the bullet she took to the head in that dark landfill, tears away the illusion Night City had built around her. V now knows that her time is slowly and irreversibly running out. And that realization becomes the first step in a long journey that slowly changes her ambition and the way she sees life and what truly matters.

The other paths the game offers confront you with the cost of becoming a legend. Trust Arasaka and you find yourself locked inside that orbital clinic, separated from your identity, your life, and the things that made you who you were, until you become little more than a corporate experiment.

text: Even when you conquer everything in The Sun ending, reach the summit of Night City and touch the sun, you can still end up completely alone in the freezing void of space. The summit becomes the city's most magnificent, yet coldest, graveyard. And then, as the credits roll, the holo calls from your friends begin to play. Judy's tearful voice, Panam's fierce and desperate tone... They all point toward the same truth: the legacy you leave behind is not a soulless name carved into neon, but the lives you touched and the people who miss you when you are gone.
title: Cyberpunk 2077 — review 234898791

text:
And this is exactly where Cyberpunk 2077's 5th Anniversary “City of Legends” trailer places V's entire journey before us, almost like pieces of the same realization. Story

The story of Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best I have ever experienced in a game. From the very beginning, it was hard to imagine where it would lead and what would happen next.

The game stays with you even after you finish it. You keep thinking about what happened, the characters, their decisions, and the choices you made.

Cyberpunk 2077 explores many important topics: life and death, friendship, loss, loneliness, memory, the fear of being forgotten, and what it means to be yourself.

The idea of fighting for your own life isn't new, but the way CD Projekt Red used it is incredible. You literally end up with a person in your head who was once your enemy and the biggest threat to your life. However, they gradually become your friend and even try to save you.

The relationship between V and Johnny is one of the emotional cores of the game. Their relationship changes from hate and mutual distrust to real friendship.

The side quests also feel meaningful. Many tell their own stories, develop the characters and world, and sometimes even add to the main story. Because of this, Night City gradually starts to feel alive.

Night City

A Journey Through a Possible Future

There are games you play, games you finish, and then there are games that stay with you for a little longer. Cyberpunk 2077 was that kind of experience for me.

I had already played it in the past on Xbox Series S, but I never really experienced it the way I wanted to. This time was different. Playing it on PC, with ray tracing pushed to the maximum and everything my GPU could handle, finally gave me the chance to experience Night City the way I had always wanted. I also came into it with very high expectations. I already knew how much this game had to tell, how complex it could be and how much freedom it offered. I knew there was a lot to discover, but knowing all of that did not make the journey any less special.

Finding My V

One of the funniest parts of my experience is that it took me around 50 hours to really find my own way of playing. What Cyberpunk 2077 Made Me Think About

More than anything else, Cyberpunk 2077 left me with a reflection on life, choices and the future. It made me think about how different our lives can become depending on the decisions we make, and how much we are willing to fight for the things we care about.

It also made me look differently at the idea of the future itself. The world of Cyberpunk can be incredibly beautiful from a technological point of view, but what fascinated me most was the contrast between that technological progress and the human stories taking place inside it. The first time I saw the enormous mountain of garbage outside Night City, I immediately thought that this could actually be a possible future. I hope it isn't, but the fact that similar realities already exist in parts of the real world makes that image even more powerful.

Final Thoughts

I finished Cyberpunk 2077 with one feeling above everything else: Satisfaction.

Satisfaction because I finally experienced the game the way I had always wanted to.

Satisfaction because I discovered Night City piece by piece.

Satisfaction because I watched V grow, change and fight for his life.

Satisfaction because I met people I will remember.

Panam.

Johnny.

Reed.

Songbird.

Kerry.

And so many others.

I spent around 115 hours in this world.

And for a while, Night City felt real.

I explored its streets.

I listened to its stories.

I watched its lights.

I laughed.

I fought.

I chose.

I lost myself in it.

And eventually, I reached the end.

Closing the game after completing everything did not feel like simply finishing another title.

Goodbye, Night City.
