A Gentle Dystopia

Ah yes, the promised land is finally here. After a botched release and years of updates improving, expanding, and stabilizing the game along with the release of the massive Phantom Liberty expansion. All is forgiven, Polish devs. But is it? As much as there is about Cyberpunk 2077 that I like and as much as I respect the support CD Projekt Red continued to put into it. We need to talk about the massive elephant in the room that never actually left. Borrowed time.

Majora's Mask is probably one of the most famous examples of making time itself part of the gameplay. Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking.
title: Cyberpunk 2077 — review 236864903

text: Even though its three day loop, that doomsday clock is always ticking. The player constantly understands that time has value. For more modern examples, look at games like The Blood of Dawnwalker or Kingdom Come Deliverance II. Neither necessarily hangs one giant doomsday clock over the player in the same way. Instead, time becomes part of the player's agency. Dawnwalker gives you a limited amount of time before the endgame, with quests and major actions advancing that clock. Deliverance II takes a more situational approach, where certain quests and events will move forward without you if you wait too long. Personally, I think Deliverance II takes this idea a little too literally. Persona 5 is another great example. You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it.

You have a limited calendar and have to decide how to spend it. Do you improve a relationship? Work on yourself? Explore the palace? Prepare for the next major confrontation? All of these systems are asking the player some variation of the same question. What are you going to do with the time you have? And Cyberpunk presents one of the strongest possible versions of that question. When you're dying, what do you do with your time?

Apparently nothing. Get up samurai, we're going drag racing. Get up samurai, we're clearing every gig and side mission on the entire map. Get up samurai, we're going bowling. Unlike many open-world games where side quests feel like repetitive filler, Cyberpunk's side missions are so well-written and unique that they often feel like they could be part of the main storyline. No.

Despite releasing over a decade ago, GTA V still stands as one of the best open-world games available on Steam in 2026. It perfectly blends a cinematic single-player campaign, a living, interactive open world, and endless multiplayer fun, offering incredible replay value that most modern AAA titles simply cannot match.
Single-Player Experience
The offline story is the game’s greatest strength, featuring a unique three-protagonist system that remains revolutionary to this day. GTA Online: Endless Gameplay With Noticeable Flaws
GTA Online is why the game has stayed popular for over ten years. It delivers massive amounts of multiplayer content, including heists, races, stunts, businesses, and full character/vehicle customization. Regular free updates keep the game fresh, offering thousands of hours of fun especially when playing with friends.
However, the online mode has clear downsides. The in-game economy forces heavy repetitive grinding for new players, and Shark Card microtransactions feel predatory and outdated. Public lobbies still suffer from hackers, lag spikes, and occasional crashes. Solo players will find progression slow and tedious, while private lobbies with friends offer a far better experience.

And now, as I am writing this review in autumn 2026, GTAVI is coming out next month. title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236962740

text: GTA games have always been a cultural phenomenon and a major force in pushing the boundaries of gameplay, immersion and, especially, vast open worlds. And I think most people would agree that GTAV became the series' highest point in all of these areas. I should note, however, that before GTAIV I personally wasn't a fan of the series for some reason. But GTAIV changed that completely. Its new engine and more realistic approach to almost everything, combined with a serious story and a huge leap in terms of immersion, finally sold me on the series. So, when GTAV was about to be released, I decided to buy a PS3 Super Slim primarily to experience it at launch, as I had previously been a PC gamer. It's crazy to think that this was 13 years ago.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236962740

text: It's crazy to think that this was 13 years ago. So I guess now is the perfect moment to draw some conclusions about GTAV and decide how we will remember this game. Personally, I would say that in many ways this game still holds up remarkably well, despite its dated movement and shooting mechanics, which feel rather clunky by today's standards. But when talking about GTAV, we cannot ignore the elephant in the room: GTA Online. And this is where two completely opposite opinions about GTAV can coexist. There is GTAV's single-player mode: a crime comedy set in a huge and immersive open world that also serves as one of the best portrayals of Los Angeles in a video game, as well as an amazing time capsule of the early 2010s.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236962740

text: And then there is GTA Online, a rather controversial multiplayer mode, which was arguably one of the main reasons Rockstar ended up taking 13 years to release GTAVI. Back in 2013, when GTA Online first launched, I genuinely enjoyed it. It felt revolutionary for its time in terms of multiplayer and what could be achieved in an open-world game. But I think many people will agree with me that its monetization eventually ruined a large part of the experience. Not to mention how much Rockstar changed the tone of the game itself through all those updates. A good example would be the heists. The original heists were quite innovative and worked surprisingly well for their time, both in terms of gameplay and immersion.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236962740

text: But then Rockstar added the Doomsday Heist, which turned GTA into some kind of absurd spy-drama parody of itself. And, of course, much of the later content was also tied to increasingly aggressive grinding and monetization. To put it simply, today's GTA Online is a bizarre and incredibly grindy experience, filled with flying futuristic cars, flying bikes, Batmobile-like vehicles, and an enormous amount of content locked behind some of the most monotonous grinding imaginable. So, as entertaining and enjoyable as the single-player experience is, the online mode has become almost the complete opposite for me: bloated, bizarre and, ultimately, rather boring. So, this is my final take on GTAV after all these years. And because of me actually playing to get 100% achievement completition, I think it's indeed valid. If you agree with me, feel free to rate this review positively.

text:
239.4 hours on record
Last played: December 2, 2024

I don't hate Grand Theft Auto V. I had fun with it, but after 239.4 hours, I eventually realized how repetitive the experience had become. GTA V was once something I could easily spend hours playing, but over time, the appeal faded & the game started feeling less like entertainment and more like an endless checklist.

GTA Online has an enormous amount of content, but that doesn't necessarily make all of it meaningful. You earn money, buy something, use it to earn more money, unlock another item, complete another activity, then repeat the same process. There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236009284

text:
There is always another vehicle, property, business, outfit, weapon, cosmetic, event, achievement, or collectible waiting for you.

Eventually, I started asking myself: what am I actually working toward?

The biggest problem is the pursuit of exclusive & rare content. GTA Online has accumulated years of limited-time items, event rewards, promotional content, rare vehicles, clothing, liveries, tattoos, collectibles & other items. Some can still be obtained through specific requirements or returning events, while others have been removed or are no longer normally obtainable.

That creates a strange situation where someone can spend hundreds of hours trying to build the "perfect" collection, only to discover that something they wanted was tied to an event from years ago.

If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236009284

text:
If the item is no longer obtainable, there is no amount of grinding that can get it back.

That's what makes the completionist mentality particularly frustrating. You're not simply trying to finish a game. You're trying to keep up with an ecosystem that has been evolving for years, while some of its history is permanently locked behind time-limited availability.

And even the items that remain obtainable can require an enormous investment of time.

For example, GTA Online's money-making activities often involve cooldowns, preparation missions, travel, matchmaking, setup, completion, & repetition. Even one of the game's major solo money-making activities has a cooldown between finales. Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236009284

text:
Multiply that type of waiting & repetition across the countless things a player might want to purchase, unlock, or collect, and the hours add up very quickly.

My 239.4 hours alone equal roughly 9.98 full days of continuous time.

That's almost ten entire 24-hour days of my life spent inside Los Santos.

And that's only the recorded gameplay time.

It doesn't include time spent researching how to obtain items, watching guides, waiting for events, comparing prices, sitting through loading screens, or deciding what to do next.

That's where the opportunity cost becomes impossible for me to ignore.

I'm not saying video games need to be productive. They're entertainment, and entertainment has value. But once a game stops being entertaining & you're continuing only because you've already invested so much time, it becomes worth asking whether that time is better spent elsewhere.

text:
GTA Online can make that especially difficult because there is always something else to obtain.

You can never quite be finished.

Another update arrives.

Another vehicle is released.

Another business becomes available.

Another event begins.

Another exclusive item appears.

Another achievement becomes something to chase.

Then the cycle starts again.

One sequence of the game eventually replaces another.

And eventually, Grand Theft Auto VI will replace this generation's attention with a new world, new characters, new gameplay systems, new content & potentially another online ecosystem to explore. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI for November 19, 2026.

If an item is available, great.

title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236009284

text:

I also don't think GTA V deserves to be treated as a bad game because of this criticism. It has had an enormous impact on gaming, GTA V's single-player campaign remains memorable, & GTA Online has maintained an extraordinary amount of content for years.

My criticism is much simpler:

There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing.

After 239.4 hours, the repetition became difficult to overlook.

The game went from:

"What should I do today?"

to:

"What else do I still need to unlock?"

That distinction matters.

At some point, you're no longer playing because you genuinely want to. You're playing because there's another box left unchecked.

title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236009284

text:
And I don't want a game to become a second job.

My last session was December 2, 2024, and I'm comfortable leaving it there.

I don't regret every hour I spent in GTA V. I had fun, experienced the world, played with other people & made memories. But I also recognize that my time has value, and I don't want to spend hundreds more hours chasing increasingly obscure items simply because the game provides an endless list of things to obtain.

Grand Theft Auto V was fun, but it became repetitive.

GTA Online has more content than most players could reasonably exhaust, yet that abundance can also become the problem.

With GTA VI arriving, I'm choosing not to spend more of my time trying to complete an ecosystem that was never designed to truly end.

text:
Grand Theft Auto V is not just a video game; it is a monumental cultural phenomenon and a sprawling, technicolor mirror held up to the face of modern capitalism. From the moment you step into the sun-drenched, smog-choked streets of Los Santos, Rockstar Games delivers a masterclass in open-world design, storytelling, and social commentary. It captures the chaotic essence of the American Dream, chews it up, and spits it back out in a glorious explosion of high-speed chases, bullet-riddled bank heists, and dark, unfiltered humor.
At the beating heart of this epic narrative is the franchise’s most ambitious storytelling mechanic: the three-protagonist system. By weaving together the lives of three distinct criminals, the game offers a multi-layered perspective of a deeply flawed world.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 237267711

text:
By weaving together the lives of three distinct criminals, the game offers a multi-layered perspective of a deeply flawed world. There is Michael, a retired bank robber trapped in a toxic, wealthy suburban nightmare, suffocated by the boredom of his own success. Then there is Franklin, a young, ambitious street hustler trying to escape the cycle of the ghetto by climbing the ladder of organized crime. And finally, Trevor, a volatile, unhinged, and borderline psychotic meth-dealer who embodies the absolute, chaotic id of the GTA franchise itself. The ability to seamlessly switch between these characters creates a dynamic, cinematic rhythm where a tranquil day at a luxury mansion can instantly dissolve into a chaotic desert shootout.
The true star of the show, however, is the map of San Andreas itself. The attention to detail is staggering.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 237267711

text:
The attention to detail is staggering. Los Santos feels alive, reacting dynamically to the player's presence. Pedestrians yell on their cell phones, traffic clogs the freeways at rush hour, and the neon lights of Vinewood reflect beautifully off the hoods of stolen supercars. Whether you are planning a meticulously detailed, multi-stage heist, diving into the ocean depths, hijacking a military fighter jet, or simply driving down Del Perro Beach while listening to a satirical talk-radio station, the level of player freedom remains completely unmatched.
Ultimately, Grand Theft Auto V stands as a timeless masterpiece because it doesn’t just let you play in a world; it forces you to experience its madness. It is a brilliant, cynical, and wildly entertaining critique of celebrity culture, government corruption, and consumerism.

Rating: 🟢 Recommended

The Ultimate Nostalgia Trip, But Make It 60 FPS

If you had told me back in 2013, huddled over a humming, overheating PlayStation 3 with the original dualshock clacking away, that I would one day be cruising down the Vinewood Hills at a buttery-smooth 60 frames per second on Steam, I probably would have cried.

Back on the PS3, GTA V was a technical marvel. We all stared in awe at the sun setting over Los Santos, forgiving the occasional texture pop-in, the 30 FPS drops during massive explosions, and the agonizingly long loading screens where you could easily go make a sandwich while Trevor was loading in. It was a masterpiece of its generation.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236826501

text:
It was a masterpiece of its generation.

Fast forward to playing it on Steam, and it feels like meeting an old friend who just got a massive glow-up.

What’s Better on Steam?

[] Performance & Fidelity: Going from the console versions of the past to a modern PC setup is night and day. The draw distances, the crisp 1080p/4K resolution, and the fluid frame rates breathe entirely new life into a world I thought I knew by heart.
[] Mods & Customization: While the vanilla game is fantastic, the PC modding community is the real MVP. Whether it's graphical overhauls, quality-of-life tweaks, or just messing around, it adds endless replay value.

- Seamless Convenience: Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.
title: Grand Theft Auto V Legacy — review 236826501

text:
- Seamless Convenience: Having it right in your Steam library alongside your achievements, screenshots, and friends list makes jumping back into Los Santos effortless.

The Verdict

Coming back to this game after years away feels weirdly comforting. Sure, the radio ads are permanently burned into my brain, and I can still navigate the map blindfolded, but the charm hasn't faded one bit. Michael, Franklin, and Trevor are just as chaotic and entertaining as they were a decade ago.

If you’re on the fence about double-dipping or jumping over from the old console days, do it. It’s a nostalgic masterpiece that still holds its own, and experiencing it without the hardware limitations of 2013 is the ultimate way to play.

Ah ♥♥♥♥, here we go again. 🎮🔥

But I need to be honest about the PC port, because if you're reading reviews before buying, you deserve to know what you're actually signing up for.

I'm running a Ryzen 7 7800X3D and an RTX 4070 Super, so this isn't a case of underpowered hardware struggling. title: Red Dead Redemption 2 — review 235290133

text:
We're talking switching rendering APIs (DX12 vs Vulkan, pick your poison, one fixes stutter and makes audio worse, the other does the opposite), manually editing system.xml files, and installing a community-made "Stutter Fix" mod just to stop the constant hitching during normal riding. None of that should be necessary in 2026 on hardware this capable.

Even after all that, I'm still dealing with audio crackling and popping that, from what I've read, has apparently been a known, unresolved issue since launch. Turns out I'm not alone, it's a well-documented complaint that's never been properly patched.

So, do I recommend it? Yes, absolutely, because the game itself is a masterpiece and worth every bit of the hassle. Just go in knowing you might need to become a part-time PC technician first. Rockstar, please, an actual optimization pass would go a long way.

Red Dead Redemption 2

Overall Rating: 10/10 — Essential Masterpiece 👍

---

[/hr]

Overview
Red Dead Redemption 2 is not merely a video game; it is a pinnacle achievement in interactive storytelling and world design. Set at the dying end of the Wild West era in 1899, Rockstar Games crafted an unmatched cinematic epic that sets a standard for open-world games that few titles have ever managed to reach.

Narrative & Character Design
The story of Arthur Morgan and the Van der Linde gang is a masterpiece of character development, tragic themes, and emotional depth. The writing is incredibly grounded, paired with industry-leading performance capture and voice acting that brings every gang member to life. Arthur Morgan remains one of the greatest protagonists in fiction.
title: Red Dead Redemption 2 — review 235592845

text:
Arthur Morgan remains one of the greatest protagonists in fiction.

World Detail & Immersion

- Unrivaled Environment: From snow-capped mountains to murky bayous and dusty frontier towns, the world feels living, breathing, and completely independent of the player.

- Meticulous Simulation: The level of detail—dynamic weather, realistic animal behavior, hair growth systems, and subtle NPC routines—creates a sense of immersion that no other open-world game currently matches.

Gameplay & Physics

- Deliberate Pacing: The gameplay prioritizes weight and realism over instant arcade gratification. Weapon maintenance, looting animations, and horse handling all carry physical weight.

- Gunplay & Euphoria Physics: Heavy, impactful gunplay enhanced by ragdoll physics and Deadeye mechanics makes every shootout feel raw, kinetic, and cinematic.

- Activities & Crafting: Deep hunting, fishing, tracking, camping, and random world encounters offer endless distraction outside of main story missions.
title: Red Dead Redemption 2 — review 235592845

text:
- Activities & Crafting: Deep hunting, fishing, tracking, camping, and random world encounters offer endless distraction outside of main story missions.

Visuals & Audio Masterpiece
Visually, the game has aged like fine wine. Combined with DLSS/FSR support and flexible PC graphics settings, the lighting, volumetric clouds, and draw distances are breathtaking. Complementing this is a dynamic, hauntingly atmospheric musical score that elevates every moment.

Red Dead Online (Current State)
While Rockstar Games has shifted core development focus away from major content expansions for Red Dead Online, the existing multiplayer suite still offers over a hundred hours of great fun for new players. The Specialist Roles (Bounty Hunter, Trader, Collector, Moonshiner), story missions, and open-world roaming with friends are fantastic, though public lobbies can occasionally suffer from peer-to-peer connection quirks or modders.

text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of those rare games that makes almost everything else feel smaller after you finish it.

The world doesn’t feel like a map filled with objectives. It feels alive. You can ride through the mountains at sunrise, get caught in a random storm, stumble into some completely unexpected encounter, and somehow lose an hour without touching a single mission. Even the smallest details feel like they were made by people who genuinely cared about the world they were building.

Arthur Morgan is easily one of the best-written characters I’ve ever played as. Watching him change throughout the story makes the game hit way harder than I ever expected. By the end, these characters don’t feel like NPCs anymore. You know their personalities, their problems, their relationships, and you actually care about what happens to them.

Sitting around the campfire, riding across an empty field, stopping in a small town, or just listening to Arthur talk to his horse somehow becomes memorable.

And visually, it’s still ridiculous. There are moments where I’ll stop riding just because the scenery looks like a painting.

This isn’t just a great open-world game. It’s one of the few games I’ve played where finishing the story actually felt like saying goodbye to people and places I had spent real time with.

If you rush through it, you’ll probably enjoy it.

An absolute cinematic triumph that trades fast-paced arcade action for unmatched open-world realism and emotional depth.

If you go into Red Dead Redemption 2 expecting a wild, high-speed "GTA in the Wild West," the initial hours will shock you—and then completely captivate you. Rockstar Games crafted what is arguably the most breathtakingly detailed, scenic open world ever put into a video game. From the misty, snow-capped peaks of Ambarino to the sun-drenched plains of New Hanover and the oppressive, murky swamps of Lemoyne, simply riding your horse through the countryside is a spiritual experience. The atmospheric lighting, dynamic weather systems, and living wildlife ecosystem make the world feel terrifyingly real. Combined with an extraordinary, slow-burn story following Arthur Morgan and the Van der Linde gang, it delivers a deeply tragic, masterfully written narrative that will stay with you long after the credits roll.

The Van der Linde camp acts as a living, breathing emotional anchor where characters converse, sing around the fire, and react dynamically to your actions and Honor level. **One of the worst control schemes I've encountered in a modern game**

Red Dead Redemption 2 is an incredible-looking game with an amazing world, story, characters, and attention to detail—but the controls are unnecessarily complicated, unintuitive, and at times downright frustrating.

The biggest problem is that the game seems to have been designed around an enormous number of context-sensitive actions rather than intuitive controls. Your character constantly has different actions mapped to the same buttons depending on what you're looking at, where you're standing, what you're holding, or what the game thinks you should be doing. Simple things like walking through a door, getting on a horse, picking something up, talking to someone, looting a body, or interacting with an object can become an exercise in figuring out which button the game wants you to press this time.
title: Red Dead Redemption 2 — review 237231115

text:
The controls also frequently feel like they're fighting against the player. Arthur can feel sluggish and overly deliberate, basic movements can require multiple inputs, and the game often interprets your input differently than you intended. There are times when you want to perform one simple action and end up doing something completely different because several contextual actions are competing for the same controls.

The keyboard and mouse implementation is particularly disappointing. For a PC game, the controls feel like they were built around a console controller and then adapted to keyboard and mouse rather than properly designed for PC. There are far too many commands, awkward key combinations, and inconsistent interactions, while some basic functions aren't nearly as intuitive as they should be.

Red Dead Redemption 2 isn't a game you play. It's a game you live.

This is possibly the most believable and alive open world I've ever experienced in a video game. Not simply because of its incredible attention to detail, but because of the people who inhabit it. The hidden conversations, the random encounters, the little interactions around camp, the relationships between characters. Everything feels organic, as if the world exists independently of you.

text:
These weren't just NPCs waiting around for the player to trigger a mission. They felt like actual people, with their own personalities, relationships and lives. And I think that says everything about the quality of the writing.

Then there's Arthur Morgan.

For me, quite possibly the greatest video game protagonist of all time.

Arthur embodies that classic image of the American cowboy, the Marlboro Man. Tough, masculine, loyal, a man who lives by his own code. But what makes him such a fascinating character is that beneath that image lies someone far more complicated.

He's not a particularly good person, especially at the beginning of the story, but that's largely because the life he leads is the only one he's ever known. His morality is shaped by the people who raised him, his loyalty to them, and the values he's spent his entire life believing in.

text:
The pacing is undeniably slow, and I understand why some people might find it tedious, especially in an age where everything seems designed to grab our attention every five seconds.

But that's precisely what makes RDR2 special.

The game allows itself to breathe.

It gives you time to get to know these people, understand their motivations, and develop genuine emotional connections with them. My playthrough took around 90 hours, and not once during the main story did I feel like I was waiting for the game to end. I was completely invested in the journey.

Even the gameplay reinforces this philosophy. The slower animations, taking care of your horse, eating, smoking, maintaining your weapons and all those little RPG mechanics might seem unnecessary on paper, but together they add another layer of immersion.
title: Red Dead Redemption 2 — review 237235575

text:
None of these systems are particularly demanding, nor are they meant to be. They're simply there to make you feel more connected to Arthur and the world around him. Smoking a cigarette to recover a stat or stopping for a meal might not sound particularly exciting, but these small interactions make the world feel more tangible.

It's not about making every individual mechanic exciting. It's about making the overall experience believable.

The soundtrack also deserves enormous praise. Music is such an important part of storytelling for me, and RDR2 understands exactly when to use it. It can be heartbreaking, uplifting, energetic, or even playful, always complementing the emotional weight of the moment. Some of the most memorable moments in the entire game wouldn't have nearly the same impact without its incredible musical direction.

text:
My only real criticism concerns the epilogue. I understand its purpose, especially as a bridge to the original Red Dead Redemption, and I appreciate the additional context it provides. However, emotionally, the main story had already reached its conclusion for me. I was still processing everything that had happened, and the slower pace of the epilogue felt less justified. I think it could have been considerably shorter without losing its impact.

As for the ending of the main story, I genuinely struggle to find the words to describe how brilliantly executed it is. From the performances to the writing, the cinematography and the emotional payoff, everything comes together beautifully. It's the culmination of dozens of hours spent living alongside these characters, and it delivers an experience that will stay with me for a very long time.

text:
Ultimately, Red Dead Redemption 2 is much more than a story about outlaws and the dying American frontier. It's a story about loyalty, family, identity, morality and what it truly means to be a good man.

But above all, it's a world that makes you care about the people living in it. And perhaps its greatest achievement is making you feel like you've actually lived through it all.

When I originally finished RDR2, I considered it a 9/10. As much as I loved the experience, I felt that other games had delivered a stronger emotional impact. text:
To no one's surprise, the game is hella realistic. It sure is sluggish compared to many games on the market, and it has a slow feel to it, but it definitely has its own charm once you start investing yourself in the game. The missions are varied enough that it never feels stale at any point, in my opinion. The gameplay isn't groundbreaking, but it is the perfect style for this type of game.

It handles its open world exceptionally well—everywhere you go feels alive. Whether you are in a town or out in the wilderness, you'll always witness something interesting, where so many other open-world games fail to deliver anything at all.

It also does a great job offsetting open-world fatigue by offering fast travel whenever the pacing starts to feel slow (like avoiding another long ride right after finishing a heavy mission). It simply does a perfect job covering up its inevitable weaknesses, and it really feels like a game made by actual gamers.

Visuals. This game is honestly breathtaking to look at. From the way light filters through the trees to the land, snow physics, and realistic weather, every frame looks like it was drawn by hand. text:

text:
Hollow Knight Review

Rating: 9.5/10

Hollow Knight is one of those games that starts relatively simple and slowly reveals just how much depth it has. What initially looks like a traditional 2D Metroidvania quickly turns into a massive, atmospheric adventure filled with exploration, challenging combat, secrets and surprisingly deep lore.

A World Worth Getting Lost In

Hallownest is easily the game's greatest achievement. The interconnected world is enormous, beautifully designed and filled with hidden paths, mysterious characters and optional areas. There is very little hand-holding, which makes discovering a new location or unlocking a previously inaccessible path incredibly satisfying.
title: Hollow Knight — review 235128741

text:
There is very little hand-holding, which makes discovering a new location or unlocking a previously inaccessible path incredibly satisfying.

The atmosphere is equally impressive. Despite being presented entirely in 2D, Hallownest feels like a real, forgotten kingdom. Abandoned cities, dark caves and mysterious ruins all tell parts of the story without constantly explaining everything to the player.

Combat & Bosses

The combat is simple to understand but difficult to master. Attacks feel responsive, and movement is precise enough that deaths usually feel like the player's fault rather than the game's.

The boss fights are some of the strongest parts of the experience. They require players to learn patterns, improve their positioning and react quickly. Some encounters are genuinely brutal, but finally defeating a boss after several attempts is extremely rewarding.
title: Hollow Knight — review 235128741

text:
Some encounters are genuinely brutal, but finally defeating a boss after several attempts is extremely rewarding.

The Biggest Strength: Exploration

Hollow Knight understands what makes exploration exciting. The game constantly gives you reasons to wonder what is behind the next door, below the next platform or at the end of an unexplored tunnel.

New abilities also completely change how you interact with the world. Areas that seemed inaccessible hours earlier suddenly become reachable, encouraging you to revisit locations and search for secrets.

The Weaknesses

The game is not perfect.

Its difficulty can be frustrating, especially during certain boss fights and platforming sections. Some players may also struggle with the lack of direction. Hollow Knight rarely tells you exactly where to go, which is great for exploration but can occasionally leave you completely lost.
title: Hollow Knight — review 235128741

text:
Hollow Knight rarely tells you exactly where to go, which is great for exploration but can occasionally leave you completely lost.

Backtracking can also become tedious, particularly when you are trying to reach a specific location after dying.

The story is another potential weakness. Much of the lore is intentionally vague and hidden inside dialogue and environmental details. Players who prefer straightforward storytelling may find it difficult to understand what is actually happening.

Art & Sound

Visually, Hollow Knight is fantastic. Its hand-drawn art style gives every area a distinct identity, while the animations make even simple enemies feel alive.

The soundtrack complements the world perfectly. Quiet exploration themes create a feeling of loneliness and mystery, while boss music makes important encounters feel appropriately dramatic.

Final Verdict

Hollow Knight is an exceptional Metroidvania that combines exploration, combat and atmosphere better than most games in the genre.
title: Hollow Knight — review 235128741

text:
Its difficulty, occasional backtracking and deliberately vague storytelling can be frustrating, but these problems are relatively minor compared to everything the game does right.

Most importantly, Hollow Knight makes exploration feel meaningful. It trusts the player to get lost, experiment and discover things without constantly pointing them toward the next objective.

Final Score: 9.5/10

Pros:
• Incredible world design and exploration
• Excellent combat
• Fantastic boss fights
• Beautiful art style
• Outstanding soundtrack
• Huge amount of content
• Rewarding progression

Cons:
• Can be extremely difficult
• Some frustrating backtracking
• Limited guidance can lead to confusion
• Storytelling can be too vague for some players

Verdict: Hollow Knight is a masterpiece of the Metroidvania genre. Its challenging combat, enormous world and incredible atmosphere make it an experience that is easy to recommend, even years after its release.

I believe the game's difficulty is for everyone. It has a low skill floor and an immensely high skill celing. The speedruns, self imposed runs, game's own challenges, they all showcase just how deep the combat system can go.
Difficulty is highly subjective but I don't think it requires much to simply beat the game considering I was able to pick & play and do all its crazy challenges without any prior experience with a metroidvania, platformer (except Celeste) or even a sidescrolling real time combat system. But ofc, the deeper you go, the more it demands.
title: Hollow Knight — review 236383197

text:
But ofc, the deeper you go, the more it demands.

The story is vague and mysterious and you will likely have to use interjection to fill in the gaps, which depending on the people can either be annoying or (for me) empowering. The game doesn't hand you much in a silver platter, you have to work for its story and so much can be found & gleaned from the unlikeliest of places, hidden in secrets within secrets.
The great part is that the story that is here, it's all purposeful. It is not a mystery for the sake of it, There is enough intentionality put in that you won't feel the game is spiraling nowhere. I am in love with its story, characters, the setting and the presentation.

title: Hollow Knight — review 235929316

text:
It teaches you everything you need to know to handle difficult bosses through exploration. And this continues throughout the game, I think that for every single boss in the game (except for the final bosses and dream bosses) the game prepares you for at least one of their attacks simply by exploring the area they're in. You will always find at least one enemy that has an attack similar to what the boss for that area will have. It's so simple in terms of game design, but genius, because it allows players like me with little to experience with combat games to be able to succeed.

text:
Left 4 Dead 2 is a game about teamwork, survival, and discovering exactly how quickly four people can completely abandon the concept of teamwork.

The premise is simple.

You're trapped in the middle of a zombie apocalypse.

There are thousands of infected.

You have guns.

Your objective is to get from point A to point B without becoming zombie food.

Easy.

Until you play with friends.

The game starts off fairly calm. You grab a weapon, pick up some supplies, and start walking through whatever horrible place the survivors have been thrown into this time.

Then someone shoots a car.

Everyone looks at them.

“Why did you shoot the car?”

“I didn't know it would make noise.”

The alarm starts.

text:
The alarm starts.

Hundreds of zombies appear.

Everyone starts screaming.

Welcome to Left 4 Dead 2.

The special infected are what make the game so much fun. Regular zombies are bad enough, but then you hear a noise and realize something much worse is coming.

Smoker?

Someone's getting dragged away.

Hunter?

Someone's getting tackled.

Boomer?

Congratulations, you're covered in vomit.

Charger?

There goes your teammate.

Jockey?

Someone is being ridden into a wall.

Tank?

RUN.

The Tank is the game's way of asking whether your team has actually been paying attention.

Usually, the answer is no.

You hear the music.

Everyone freezes.

“Tank.”

Someone says it quietly.

You all immediately start running in different directions.

One person gets separated.

Someone falls off a ledge.

Great teamwork.

The campaign design is also fantastic. Every level feels like a journey rather than just a collection of rooms, and you're constantly moving toward some kind of safe room while trying to survive whatever the Director decides to throw at you.

And that's one of the best parts of the game.

The game seems to know exactly when you're getting comfortable.

You haven't seen anything dangerous for a while.

Your health is good.

You have plenty of ammunition.

You start thinking:

“This is going pretty well.”

Then the Director decides that you're having too much fun.

A horde appears.

The AI Director keeps every game feeling slightly different, which is a huge reason L4D2 has remained so replayable.

You can play the same campaign multiple times and still have completely different experiences.

Maybe you get attacked by three special infected simultaneously.

Maybe your friend gets dragged into a hole and you have to rescue them.

Left 4 Dead 2: The Immortal King of Co-op Zombie Shooters
When Valve released Left 4 Dead 2 in 2009, barely a year after its predecessor, skeptics wondered if it was too soon for a sequel. Fast forward to today, and the game stands as an undeniable masterpiece that has stubbornly refused to age. It isn't just one of the best zombie games ever made; it is the definitive cooperative shooter experience, setting a gold standard that countless studios have tried—and failed—to replicate.

The AI Director 2.0: The Puppet Master
The beating heart of Left 4 Dead 2 is its dynamic pacing, governed by the ingeniously upgraded "AI Director 2.0". This system observes how well your team is performing and alters the level layout, item spawns, weather, and enemy waves on the fly. If you are breezing through a level, the Director might summon a torrential downpour to ruin your visibility, followed immediately by a devastating horde. If your team is limping toward the safehouse with single-digit health, the Director might show a rare moment of mercy, spawning a clutch bottle of pain pills in a side room. This mechanic ensures that no two playthroughs of the same campaign ever feel identical, creating an endless loop of unscripted, water-cooler moments.

A Masterclass in Audio and Enemy Design
To survive the apocalypse, you have to listen. Valve's sound design in Left 4 Dead 2 is nothing short of brilliant, serving as both atmosphere and a vital gameplay mechanic. Every Special Infected has a distinct audio cue that triggers pure panic: the hacking cough of a Smoker, the shrill screech of a Hunter, the gurgling of a Boomer, or the terrifying, screen-shaking roar of an incoming Tank. The sequel introduced three new Special Infected that completely changed the tactical landscape:
The Charger: A hulking brute that punishes teams who bunch up in narrow corridors, charging through them like bowling pins.
The Spitter: A terrifying area-denial zombie that forces survivors out of tight, defensive corners with pools of burning acid.

The Jockey: A manic, giggling gremlin that leaps onto your back and steers you directly into danger or off ledges.
The synergy between these monsters means players are constantly forced to communicate. If a Smoker drags your medic away while a Spitter cuts off your path to save them, your team has mere seconds to adapt or die.
Carnage with Character
The game trades the original's grim, cinematic darkness for a sun-drenched, blood-soaked road trip through the American South. The new cast—Nick, Rochelle, Coach, and Ellis—bring an endless amount of charm and wit to the grim setting. Their banter feels natural and evolves as the campaign progresses, seamlessly providing lore and comic relief without slowing down the action.

Perhaps the most staggering thing about Left 4 Dead 2 is its immense longevity. text:
Left 4 Dead 2 is commonly referred to as a sequel done right, as people claim it improves on every aspect of the original game in all the right ways.

I do agree with that for the most part, as the game features new weapons, infected, and creative level design, but I also think the gameplay gets ruined by how the infected have been tuned to be much, much sweatier compared to the original game, especially when playing on Expert or Expert Realism difficulties. Normal infected try to either hit you from the back, or run to the side of your field of vision, which feels very videogamey and fake difficultey, and that breaks immersion. Also the spawns of the special infected oftentimes feel rigged and undodgeable compared to how they felt in the first game, especially for hunter, jockey and charger.
title: Left 4 Dead 2 — review 237401723

Also the spawns of the special infected oftentimes feel rigged and undodgeable compared to how they felt in the first game, especially for hunter, jockey and charger.

The frustrations with the difficulty have outweighed the positives for me in the long run, as I felt like I wasn't really fighting against a gameplay challenge that I had to overcome, but rather the flawed logic that the developers had, by which making the enemies tankier and harder to react to on higher difficulties is a good way of creating said difficulty.

I'd recommend purchasing the first game over this one, as it feels like a tighter, more simplistic, and less overwhelming experience that still has all the core aspects that Left 4 Dead franchise is known for (the impressive facial animations, the co-op aspect, the atmosphere, the tension of hordes of zombies coming at you, etc.)

Left 4 Dead is an absolute blast with friends.

This game is a 16-year-old piece of software that still somehow runs better than half the modern live-service slop being released today. Congrats, Valve. Your ancient zombie shooting gallery from the Obama administration still hits harder than most $70 “AAA experiences.”
The AI Director will either drown you in a tidal wave of Special Infected the second you dare to breathe near a safe room, or it will fall asleep and leave you wandering empty streets like a lonely sad bastard for ten minutes. The Specials still have the pathfinding intelligence of a concussed raccoon. Smokers will drag you through walls. Chargers will yeet you into the void. text:
And the Tank? The Tank will clip through geometry, no-scope you from three maps away, and then despawn out of pure spite.
Versus mode is a gladiatorial arena of pure toxicity where half the lobby is cheating, the other half is throwing, and everyone is screaming racial slurs in voice chat. It’s beautiful.
Yet here I am. 121 hours later. Still loading up this dusty old relic every time I want to feel something. Because when the chaos clicks—when your team is coordinated, the Director is on one, and you’re screaming while a Tank is chasing you through a burning building with a chainsaw—nothing else comes close.
It’s janky. It’s old. It’s held together with duct tape and Valve’s pure refusal to let it die.
And I still love it.

text:
A genre-defining co-op zombie shooter that's still one of the best ways to spend a night with three friends and a chainsaw. The Special Infected roster (Charger, Spitter, Jockey) forces actual teamwork instead of everyone just standing in a corner mowing down waves, and the Director AI still does a solid job of never letting a run feel scripted twice.

It also doubles as a great friendship test: nothing reveals someone's true character quite like watching them "accidentally" leave you behind the exact second a Tank shows up.

The honest complaint since day one was that this felt like it should've been a paid expansion for the first game rather than a full sequel — and that's fair.
title: Left 4 Dead 2 — review 235436587

A lot of it is L4D1 refined rather than reinvented. But refined is still really good, and the campaigns (Dead Center, the Hard Rain storm finale especially) hold up more than a decade later.

Recommended if you've got friends willing to actually communicate instead of running off solo into a horde (see: friendship test, above).

It's also supposed to be a fast-paced game, but honestly, it felt pretty slow to me. There were moments where I expected the gameplay to be much more exciting and intense, but instead, it felt like everything took longer than it should have.

Umbrella Corps started as Capcom’s attempt at creating a competitive squad-based online shooter, and it ended up as a cheap-looking, repetitive, and desolate mess.

Long version:

For a game that was supposed to rival Overwatch at its launch, Umbrella Corps manages to impress us only with its spectacular list of failures.

text:
The list could go in infinitely, but it would be moot anyway, since the online portion of Umbrella Corps on PC died two weeks after launch.

As for the single-player part, it is a series of 24 challenges, spread across the seven available maps. These are just barebones horde mode with some flavour text, a predetermined loadout, and a mixture of three possible objectives. text:
Umbrella Corps

Introduction to a Broken Game

I am pretty confident that almost every gamer is aware of the famous Umbrella Corporation from the Resident Evil series. This is a game that was made and published by the makers of Resident Evil themselves, CAPCOM. It’s clearly evident that the game has a lot of hate on Steam as its review section is filled with hate comments/reviews. In my opinion, this game deserves the hate, but not this much. I mean, I really liked the gameplay, although it’s highly repetitive, broken, janky, and may get boring after a short while. Capcom basically brought up good ideas in this game and they also brought those ideas crashing down due to broken gameplay.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 89135340

text:
Capcom basically brought up good ideas in this game and they also brought those ideas crashing down due to broken gameplay.

Game Information

Storyline

This game doesn’t follow an actual storyline. You basically play as a mercenary named 3A7 who carries out objectives under the supervision of two Umbrella Corps Employees; Abraham Jackson and Beatrice Bertrand.

Gameplay Mechanics

This is one of the major fields in which CAPCOM messed up real bad. This game has terrible mechanics. First off, the camera placement is really awkward. It’s not in First-Person or the normal Third-Person. The camera is placed a bit right to the right shoulder of the player. You get a kind of side view.

Well, shooting is not a problem since as long as you get the enemies inside your crosshair, you are guaranteed to hit them.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 89135340

text:
Well, shooting is not a problem since as long as you get the enemies inside your crosshair, you are guaranteed to hit them. The gunplay is smooth but the weapons are a bit too accurate. The main problem of wielding firearms is that when you scope in, there is a lot of movement penalty. Your, rather fast, character starts moving very slowly. Another problem with the guns is that the reloading time is tremendous. They take too long to reload, which can throw you into a disadvantageous situation if you have terrible aim.

Thirdly, Melee attacks are overpowered. Your normal melee attack is powerful enough to take down more than one enemy in one hit, most of the time whereas guns take several bullets to take down a zombie unless it’s a headshot.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 89135340

text: Players on the other hand are literally bullet sponges and would take a ♥♥♥♥ ton of bullets to down an opponent. In addition to that, it greatly increases your movement when compared to wielding a firearm. Since players are literal bullet sponges, you can run towards a player who is emptying their magazine at you while wielding your Debrainer and take them out. Although most of your equipment works against you, the overpowered Debrainer is the only trusty ally you have.

The infamous Umbrella Corps. I bought this game as a joke and in order to have all resident evil games on steam. Now I played it a lot. Mostly with community made matches that were pre organized or through a few friends I made. I think the release of this is just funny what they tried to achieve with resident evil despite having actually some interesting mechanics to offer.

Gameplay
Surprisingly the movement in this game is absolutely great. You can vault over anything, climb on a second floor in a really neat animation and even lay down and crawl at a decent speed. The whole game is really quick and its fun to move around.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 155288189

text:
The whole game is really quick and its fun to move around. Shooting works decent as well, switching into a first-person mode for better aim at will. Due to the bad internet connection with most players, often the hit feedback just sucks so people tend to die at the same time or suddenly. There is a fun melee system in there which caused me to play with people melee only via the pickaxe.
That is the only positives I can say. Its just that the gameplay and modes just don’t work in any way good together.

There are zombies on the map which attack you incase a player shoots your transmitter which makes zombies ignore you.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 155288189

text:
There are zombies on the map which attack you incase a player shoots your transmitter which makes zombies ignore you. A whole lot of encounters end due to one player shooting that thing, the other dies and both die because suddenly 99% of the map comes sprinting at the player and the zombies keep respawning at a very fast pace. Rarely you can manage to kill a player and replace your transmitter, in public games I managed to do it once or twice in my few dozen matches.

Additionally, the systems of the game don’t work that well together with the modes. It completely screws some teams over. Having a vip protect mission? Go into a corner of the map while one guy stays behind and two people cover him. Due to third person, they can protect places and shoot around corners without any problem.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 155288189

text:
Due to third person, they can protect places and shoot around corners without any problem.

The game focuses more on being a competitive game due to its 3 vs 3 setup. They seriously tried to make this an e-sport of some sort. Yeah in a game that has so many easy ways to exploit certain stages it would have been funny to see people camp in corners and shoot around them while people try to capture a point.
There is also a brutally hard singleplayer mode which just gives the player specific challenges which are mostly luck based or by exploiting the enemy ai as there is no way anyone playtested this.

A lot of the things in the game just feel like an asset flip, considering it was made with unity im not surprised.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 155288189

text:
But the final nail in the coffin for me was that there is no server/lobby browser. All is done via matchmaking. Which is super annoying to play multiple games in row since the waiting time is a large chunk of your total playtime due to matches being short anyways,

Story
There is none. Testing is mentioned but what this implies actually no idea. The sp does not really offer anything of value in that regard.

Sound
I did not remember anything except the main menu theme (due to matchmaking being impossible) and some of the completely stock combat sound effects.

Graphics
It’s okay, I guess? But in a multiplayer game visibility is important. This one is so drab in its colour scheme that hard to make out enemies. Whole game just looks average at best.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 155288189

text:
Whole game just looks average at best.

Conclusion/TL;DR
A seriously unique, awful and forgettable multiplayer experience. I don’t really know why anyone thought it was a good idea to release this game, considering it plays like a bad mp side mode in a singleplayer game but they ask a hefty price for this one.

Totally unbalanced and dead multiplayer game. Avoid

My Honest Review: Great Potential, Disastrous Launch
Overall Rating: 6.5/10 (Average)

I’m sure some of you were expecting a glowing review from me, but unfortunately, I can't provide one yet. I wish there were a "neutral" option on this platform, but since I have to choose, I cannot recommend the game in its current state.

The Core Experience
The game is actually very fun to play. On Day 1, it was exciting to see so many people jumping in. However, like many releases from major companies lately, the launch has been a disaster. The game itself isn't terrible—it’s actually quite good—but the technical issues are holding it back.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 23731262

text:
The game itself isn't terrible—it’s actually quite good—but the technical issues are holding it back.

The Technical Issues (The Dealbreakers)
1. Poor Mouse Input The mouse controls feel like they were ported directly from an Xbox controller. This makes aiming up and down feel sluggish and unnatural. It’s a major handicap in a game that requires precision, and I hope a fix is released soon.

2. Connection & Party Problems Trying to play as a team is a nightmare. If you leave a party and try to rejoin, you often aren’t placed back on the same team. To fix this, you have to remake the entire lobby, but even then, I frequently get disconnected as soon as we start searching for a match. This isn't an internet issue on my end, as rejoining works fine—the matchmaking system is simply unstable.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 23731262

text:
This isn't an internet issue on my end, as rejoining works fine—the matchmaking system is simply unstable.

3. Lobby Limit Bugs This is the most frustrating issue: the last person to join the lobby (the 6th player) almost always gets kicked or disconnected. It makes full-party sessions nearly impossible to maintain.

The Verdict
The Positive: Once you actually get into a match, it’s a blast. The moments are intense, the gameplay is engaging, and the game has massive potential if the developers support it correctly.

The Negative: The bugs are currently killing the player base. By Day 2, the player count already started to drop, likely because people can't get the game to start or are fed up with the mouse controls.

text:
Forgotten Resident Evil multiplayer TPS

   ★★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆

Umbrella Corps is a lesser-known multiplayer-focused addition to the Resident Evil family, owing part of its obscurity to the fact that it is the only title in the gargantuan franchise whose title does not include the name of the actual series it is part of. It is almost as if someone didn't actually wanted it to be associated with other Resident Evil games, for one reason or another. The result? An utterly forgettable but fairly decent and even somewhat innovative third-person shooter with nostalgic throwbacks to the most popular entries of the franchise.

“This advanced training shows us the subject's true potential. It also determines whether the lab rat lives or dies.

text:
It also determines whether the lab rat lives or dies.

Life or death... in this arena, they're almost the same anyway.”

I've pretty much only heard bad things about Umbrella Corps before playing it - from very negative reviews from mainstream publications, to Mostly Negative rating on Steam - everyone seems to be advising that this should not be given a second look. While I am not planning to go against grain in this review, I have to admit that I did enjoy Umbrella Corps a lot more than I expected (certainly more than the more recent multiplayer-only titles). That came from two things - well-designed shooting model and the nostalgia-bait in the form of the most recognizable of maps from Resident Evil 4, 5, and even 3 and 1.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 192350426

text:
Not going to lie - being able to re-visit these locations in a more modern engine was a nice blast from the past, even if it is ultimately pointless because in the grand scheme of Resident Evil things, what little happened in this game is completely irrelevant, despite it supposedly being canon.

The most relevant reason why you would want to avoid this game is the obvious - it's completely dead. It is a multiplayer-first game relying on an active player base which is all but gone. All of my hours in-game came from the supremely limited single-player content which sees you repeat the three quasi-multiplayer gamemodes solo through its all 5-6 maps.
title: Umbrella Corps — review 192350426

text:
As I mentioned above, this IS enjoyable to the extent that you experiment with the gameplay and different weapons killing different enemies in different maps as quickly as you can. It is fairly challenging too as you can die from 2-hits and the enemies are fairly agile and aggressive. Apart from that though, this is something that was designed purely as a tutorial and a practice for the actual matches, which you can't get into nowadays.

Concluding this – save your money, time, and patience. Unless you are a completionist freak like me and absolutely want to at least experience every single Resident Evil game, don't bother. There is nothing here that you won't find better elsewhere, and if you crave the nostalgia trip, then just go back to those individual games and play them for the umpteenth time. You'll have better life.

A Unique Spin on the Resident Evil Universe!

Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)

I was pleasantly surprised by my experience with Umbrella Corps! As a long-time Resident Evil fan, I was excited to see how this game would integrate the elements I love into a more competitive multiplayer environment - and it did not disappoint!

The fast-paced gameplay is a breath of fresh air compared to the traditional Resident Evil titles. The tactical elements add depth, and the emphasis on teamwork makes each match thrilling. I found myself strategizing with teammates and really getting into the competitive spirit. The maps are well-designed, offering a mix of close-quarters combat and open areas that keep you on your toes.

text:
The variety of weapons and gear allows for customization that fits my play style perfectly. I especially love the ability to use a zombie as a distraction – it adds a fun layer of strategy. The blend of horror elements with competitive gameplay really captures the essence of the Resident Evil franchise while offering a unique twist.

Graphics and sound design are top-notch, creating an immersive atmosphere that perfectly captures the creepy vibes of the Resident Evil world. It's always thrilling to hear the moans of zombies lurking nearby as you strategize your next move!

While it's not a traditional Resident Evil experience, Umbrella Corps has carved out its niche and offers a fantastic way for fans to enjoy the franchise in a new light. If you’re looking for something different that maintains the spooky charm of Resident Evil, I highly recommend giving it a shot!

text:
Umbrella Corps is an RE spin-off that seemingly wants to compete with games like Left 4 Dead. it‘s a coop third-person-shooter with zero variation. it gives you only three basic objectives:
1: kill a certain amount of zombies and collect the DNA samples they drop after their defeat.
2: collect five briefcases scattered around the map.
3: get to five different areas on the map and defend them all for about 15 seconds.
you won’t do anything remotely different. just those three things. over and over and over again.

not only that there is nearly no variation in the objectives. the rest of the game is equally sparse: there are basically only about half a dozen very small and boring maps and the enemy roster is limited to zombies and zombie dogs (and really annoying crows on a few maps, if you want to count them).

so many things in this game feel completely useless and you‘ll constantly just ask yourself: „why? what is this for? what is the purpose of this? what am i playing?“

the grenades are useless because they barely do any damage.
the sprint- and crouch-buttons, radar and minimap are almost completely useseless since you simply never use all this sh*t.
the cover system is useless since you only fight zombies and zombie dogs that (surprise, surprise) have no weapons and don’t shoot back.

text:
Call of Duty: Warzone - Frustratingly Bloated Bad Experience

Call of Duty: Warzone has the foundation of a great battle royale, but in its current state, it feels increasingly difficult to enjoy. One of the most immediate and frustrating issues isn’t even gameplay-related, it’s the installation. To play Warzone, which itself only takes around 30–50GB, players are forced to install over 200GB of game files!! This massive download often includes unnecessary content and bloatware from multiple Call of Duty integrations, making it extremely inconvenient for players with limited storage.

Beyond that, the core experience is suffering. Based on recent player feedback and analysis, Warzone currently faces several major problems, with the most significant being a combination of persistent cheating and unstable server performance.
title: Call of Duty: Warzone — review 221680362

text:
These issues are made worse by the yearly integration of new Call of Duty titles, which continue to introduce more technical problems and unnecessary complexity into the game.

Cheating remains one of the biggest concerns. Despite the Ricochet anti-cheat system, players frequently encounter aimbots, wallhacks, and unlock tools,especially in higher-skill lobbies. The situation has become so bad that many describe the game as “unplayable,” since banned players can easily return with new accounts.

Server performance is another major issue. Lag, packet loss, and desync are common, leading to frustrating situations where shots don’t register properly. At times, it genuinely feels like you’re fighting the servers more than your opponents. On top of that, bugs such as crashes and freezes, especially during looting,further damage the experience.
title: Call of Duty: Warzone — review 221680362

text:
On top of that, bugs such as crashes and freezes, especially during looting,further damage the experience.

The constant addition of weapons and content from multiple Call of Duty titles has created severe balance issues. With so many guns, attachments, and operators, maintaining fair gameplay has become nearly impossible. This often results in stale and frustrating metas where only a handful of weapons are viable.

Audio problems also persist, with inconsistent footstep sounds and missing audio cues making it harder to react to enemies. Combined with strict skill based matchmaking (SBMM) and a high skill gap, casual players are increasingly pushed away, leaving behind a more competitive and less welcoming environment.

Finally, the yearly “reset” cycle continues to frustrate long-time players. Each new integration disrupts progress and changes core mechanics, making it hard to stay invested in the game long term.
title: Call of Duty: Warzone — review 221680362

text:
Each new integration disrupts progress and changes core mechanics, making it hard to stay invested in the game long term.

While Warzone still has moments of fun and potential, the overall experience is weighed down by bloated installations, technical issues, and recurring design problems. Unless these core issues are addressed, it’s hard to recommend the game in its current state.

text:
Call of Duty: Warzone doesn't just install, it colonizes. 125GB just to get through the front door, and that's before the "additional content" starts rolling in like an uninvited houseguest who never leaves. Season updates, content packs, "optimizations" that somehow make things bigger — it never ends. Warzone is the israel of games: it keeps expanding arrogantly disrespecting the community and disregarding how disk space is pricier and more valuable nowadays. Lack of sensibility and competency.
Who greenlit this? Who sat in a meeting and decided that a battle royale shooter needed to rival the storage footprint of an operating system archive? This isn't ambition, it's negligence dressed up as "a ton of content." Infinity Ward themselves have admitted their production pipeline "isn't perfect" — which is corporate-speak for "we know it's bad, and we're not fixing it fast enough."
title: Call of Duty: Warzone — review 235893793

text:
The sheer audacity of it:

Zero respect for SSD pricing. Fast storage isn't cheap, and Activision treats your drive like it's bottomless. One game shouldn't force you to choose between Warzone and literally everything else you own.
The bait-and-switch install. You commit to 125GB, thinking you're done — then the real download begins. It's less "game installation" and more "hostage negotiation with your free space."
No accountability for years. This isn't new. Complaints about Warzone's bloat go back to 2020, and here we are, years later, still bleeding gigabytes with every patch. "We'll optimize it" has become the industry's most hollow promise.
Shared-asset excuse doesn't cut it. Yes, Warzone shares progression with other CoD titles — but that's an engineering choice, not a law of physics.
title: Call of Duty: Warzone — review 235893793

text:
Yes, Warzone shares progression with other CoD titles — but that's an engineering choice, not a law of physics. Other live-service games manage streaming and asset compression far more gracefully.
Punishes loyalty, not rewards it. The more content they add, the more storage tax you pay — there's no cap, no ceiling, just an ever-expanding footprint with no end in sight.

At some point, "big game with lots of content" stops being an excuse and starts being a confession of poor engineering discipline. Plenty of AAA titles deliver comparable scale and visual fidelity without demanding you gut your entire drive to play one map on repeat.

Bottom line: This isn't a game, it's a storage eviction notice. Until the developers actually respect players' hardware and wallets, this is a hard pass — and an easy one-star review.

text:
A Cheap Cash-Grab Attempt on a Legendary Franchise

We all know that the Test Drive series holds a special place in the history of racing games. At least, it did until this game. Most of us still remember the luxurious atmosphere and the pure joy of freely driving around the island in the old TDU games. However, after a long silence, the developers came back with this. Unfortunately, Test Drive Unlimited: Solar Crown feels like a project designed to make quick money using a famous brand name, rather than showing respect to its great legacy.

A Horrible Story and Terrible Characters

From the moment you start playing, one question comes to mind: What were they thinking when they wrote this story?
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

text:
From the moment you start playing, one question comes to mind: What were they thinking when they wrote this story? The scenario and its presentation feel so forced that it is almost impossible to get into the game. The visual side is also a total disappointment. While expecting great graphics and smooth performance by modern standards, we are faced with character models so ugly and lifeless that I find myself hitting the "skip" button during every single cutscene.
<URL>
The character creator is lazy and completely mediocre. I just made a random character and skipped it quickly because the game gives you no reason to customize anything. On top of that, the clothing textures and character models are so low-pixel that the game feels like a mobile title from years ago. Tbh, many modern mobile racing games have much better and more detailed character models than this.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

text:
Tbh, many modern mobile racing games have much better and more detailed character models than this.

Older Games Were Much More Entertaining

When it comes to the racing mechanics and logic, things get even worse. During a race, I flew right over a checkpoint, but the game did not count it and teleported me backward. Excuse me, but even in NFS Underground, which came out back in 2000, flying over the finish line worked perfectly. Making this work is not rocket science. Did the people who made this game never play a racing game before? This is proof that companies that only care about money cannot be player-friendly. Sadly, we know that many big companies are run by people who do not understand video games.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

text:
Sadly, we know that many big companies are run by people who do not understand video games.

Having such stupid logic errors in a highly anticipated game is frustrating. Generally, driving feels very weird too. The car's handling is extremely unstable. When you brake at high speeds, the car stops almost instantly, which feels very unnatural. It is too twitchy at high speeds, and you cannot control it precisely. The legendary old TDU had a handling model that was 100 times better and more realistic.

No Optimization: Feels Like a Cheap AI Generation

The technical side of the game is an absolute disaster. Optimization simply does NOT exist. I can play the latest, most demanding games at 4K resolution on high settings with 60fps, yet I cannot even get a stable 30 FPS in Solar Crown with the same settings.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

<URL>
In this state, the game feels like it was rushed out with the help of a basic AI. It feels cheap, poorly made, and nonsensical. This is definitely not a real Test Drive experience. If this game had been released under a completely different name, people might have been more forgiving, looking at it as a studio's first attempt. But you cannot take a beloved franchise, ruin it like this, and expect positive feedback.

HUD/MENU Chaos and Some Good Details

The HUD design also looks cheap. They tried to copy other popular racing games but failed completely.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

text:
They tried to copy other popular racing games but failed completely. While driving, the permanent AI markers and the giant photo mode button on the screen are incredibly annoying. They could have easily integrated these shortcuts into the map or menus, or kept it clean and minimalist like the Forza games.

To be fair, the car sounds are actually good. They also thought about some nice mechanics. Working as a taxi driver and delivering cars to high-level executives is fun. However, all these good ideas get completely buried under terrible graphics, logic flaws, and massive technical issues. Unfortunately, the foundation of the game is broken, so these small features do not matter much.

Pros:

- Car sound designs are successful and satisfying.

- They tried some new mechanics, and the ideas behind them are good.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227599855

- Zero optimization.

Final

This game is a cash-grab that damages the reputation of a legendary franchise. Under normal circumstances, it should not have sold this much. I will keep it in my library only out of respect and love for the old Test Drive games, but playing this for a long time is out of the question. I would rather spend my time playing a racing game from 10–15 years ago and have much more fun.

text:
First, let me be clear: I bought this game at 80% off for about $10. Put that into perspective—that's the price of a decent burger or a bottle of wine these days. You enjoy it for what it's worth, and then it's gone. You're never getting that money back, and you shouldn't further analyze it as some sort of investment.

That said, the one thing that is true to the TDU franchise is the driving itself. The physics, suspension, and traction modeling are more arcade-oriented and "smoothed" (aka dulled) compared to a sim-cade game like Forza, but they're not nearly as arcade-like as NFS.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 227535136

text:
The scaling of speed feels good, but it lacks the sharpness and precision needed for quick weight transfers or snappy maneuvering. This makes driving fast feel less accurate but more comfortable. It is not for those who want super-precise traction management or a highly technical driving style... BUT—it also is not a turn-and-burn, drift-or-die experience like Need for Speed. And that makes this game unique. You can't get this kind of neutral arcade handling experience in any other driving game today, at least not one with decent graphics.

Another positive aspect is the variety of activity types. Delivery missions, Domination (endurance), Detective missions—stuff that makes for a fun driving experience aside from just straight-up wheel-to-wheel racing the entire time.

text:
Graphics and performance are FINE. I'm not running a NASA computer, and this game looks and performs about as well as any other racing title I've tried in the last five years. I really don't see much difference. The art design actually looks like it has some direction, with good weather effects and evocative lighting. The sound design is solid—unique engine sounds, a full spectrum of frequencies, and dynamic reflections. I also have not experienced any game-breaking bugs, glitches, FPS spikes, or crashes.

OK, onto the criticism—and I'm just dogpiling on a dead horse here with everyone else. None of the immersion or lifestyle factors that made TDU appealing in the past are present in this release. text:
I understand why this title has been such a huge disappointment to most people, and I feel sorry for those who paid full price at launch—but how did you not see that coming? The developers got the core driving elements in and then left the rest to burn. Fun, casual driving engine. Good graphics. Big map. All they had to do was tackle some of the core MMO elements that made TDU unique, but then they said, "♥♥♥♥ it."

There's nothing special here other than the unrealistic hope that the devs will add everything that's missing—but it's not quite as bad as the majority of people make it out to be. If you need a break from the NFS or Forza ecosystem, buy it for the price of an XXL burrito, and you might get some fun out of it.
