text:
At the most complete, as a former player of Test Drive Unlimited 2, I find it difficult to recognize the true TDU spirit in Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown.

The game feels much more like a generic open-world racing game than a genuine automotive lifestyle simulation like the older TDU titles.

First of all, the character customization and appearance system feels underdeveloped. Although clothing stores (Clans) are present, the available selection remains limited and is often focused on a single style. The game does not provide enough freedom to create a truly unique avatar or experiment with different fashion styles. Compared to the lifestyle aspect that previous TDU games emphasized, the clothing system feels superficial and clearly lacks variety.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 226650648

text:
Compared to the lifestyle aspect that previous TDU games emphasized, the clothing system feels superficial and clearly lacks variety.

Another major issue concerns vehicle management. In previous Test Drive Unlimited games, purchasing cars was directly tied to buying houses and garages. If you wanted to expand your collection, you first needed enough parking spaces, which added an extra layer of logic and progression. In Solar Crown, vehicle storage appears to be unlimited, removing an essential mechanic that encouraged players to invest in real estate and manage their collection. This ties directly into what is arguably the biggest missing feature: the complete absence of real estate. In TDU2, houses and apartments were an integral part of progression and the sense of achievement, as were the parking spaces associated with them. Here, almost everything revolves exclusively around cars and racing.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 226650648

text:
Here, almost everything revolves exclusively around cars and racing.

The in-game economy is also frustrating. Vehicles are extremely expensive while rewards are relatively low, making grinding feel inefficient and sometimes discouraging. Progression becomes so slow that owning multiple cars can require dozens or even hundreds of hours.

Several iconic features have disappeared as well, such as driving schools and the category-based license system, both of which added a real sense of progression in TDU2.

Another missing feature is the police system. In TDU2, police vehicles were part of traffic, and players could receive fines, build up a criminal record, or take part in police chases. There was even a form of progression tied to this system for players who enjoyed driving more recklessly. This aspect of gameplay has completely disappeared in Solar Crown, removing yet another mechanic that contributed to Test Drive Unlimited's unique identity.

text:
Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown: An Honest Take From a TDU2 Veteran
I'll be upfront: I was very skeptical going into Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown. That Mostly Negative reception on Steam was a real wall to climb, and it almost kept me away entirely. But curiosity got the better of me. I put serious hours into TDU2 back in the day, and I had to see for myself what this revival was actually about.

Handling
Let's start with something that surprised me positively: the handling isn't as bad as I expected. I always turn TCS off immediately, and sliding in this game is genuinely fun once you learn the feel of it. Most cars are actually pretty forgiving to control, easier than you'd think, and once it clicks, there's real satisfaction in throwing a car into a corner and catching it clean. Not a perfect system, but it works.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 228781943

text:
Not a perfect system, but it works.

Content vs. File Size
Here's where it starts to fall apart though. 100GB install size for a game with fewer cars than TDU2? That's genuinely hard to justify. TDU2 launched over a decade ago and still had more variety on the lot. The file size alone sets an expectation the game just doesn't meet.

Racing
The racing feels almost like an afterthought. Rewards are low, the incentive to grind through events barely exists, and I found myself avoiding races entirely after a while. Ironically, the taxi missions and car delivery jobs are far more rewarding, both in payouts and in just having something purposeful to do on the map. It says a lot when the side content outshines the core gameplay loop.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 228781943

text:
It says a lot when the side content outshines the core gameplay loop.

The Luxury Lifestyle Factor
This one hurts the most. TDU was always about living the fantasy: the mansions, the clothes, the social flex of driving something obscene through a beautiful open world. Solar Crown tries to gesture at that identity but never really commits to it. That soul feels diluted, like the spirit of the series got lost somewhere in development.

The Bottom Line
If you're a cruiser like me, someone who just wants to put on music, pick a direction, and drive, Solar Crown actually scratches that itch reasonably well. The island looks decent, the cars feel good enough to just be in, and there's something peaceful about free-roaming without an agenda. But if you came for the full TDU experience, you're going to feel the gaps.

I’ve been having a really good time with Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown. It’s not a perfect game, but if you enjoy open-world driving and the classic TDU vibe, there’s a lot here to like.

Graphics & Atmosphere
The cars look fantastic and are highly detailed, which is honestly one of the highlights. Cars

text:
There’s a great selection, and they all look and sound really good. More importantly, they’re just fun to drive. Whether it’s a supercar or something more casual, every car feels enjoyable in its own way. Collecting new cars is genuinely motivating, and trying them out never gets boring.

Driving & Gameplay
The handling strikes a nice balance between arcade and realism. It’s easy to pick up but still feels satisfying when you push cars to their limits. Cruising around the map can be just as fun as racing, which really fits the TDU style.

Open World
Hong Kong Island is a cool setting and feels great to explore at your own pace. The map is large enough to keep things interesting, and I’ve enjoyed just discovering new routes and taking in the scenery. It really captures that “drive wherever you want” feeling.

Multiplayer & Online
Seeing other players in the world adds to the experience and gives it a nice shared-world feeling, even if you’re just casually driving around.

Fun Factor
At the end of the day, the game is just fun. Driving, collecting cars, and relaxing in the open world makes it easy to come back to again and again.

Final Verdict
Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown delivers a fun and laid-back open-world racing experience, especially if you enjoy driving and collecting cool cars.

text:
Like many players, my experience with Test Drive Unlimited: Solar Crown at launch was deeply disappointing. For roughly three weeks, the servers were unstable, performance was poor, and the grinding system felt excessively harsh. These problems drove me away, convinced I wouldn't return until the game offered a genuinely enjoyable experience.

I decided to give it another chance during a recent free weekend. The changes implemented over the past year and across multiple seasons are significant and, frankly, expected. New features like delivery missions, taxi jobs, and the high-paying long races unlocked at Level 55 are excellent additions. Navigation missions, in particular, have become a standout method for efficiently grinding both reputation and money.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 216522421

text:
Navigation missions, in particular, have become a standout method for efficiently grinding both reputation and money. These improvements are welcome and were the primary reason I found myself drawn back in. For the first time, reaching Reputation Level 50, unlocking hypercars, and affording them felt like an achievable goal rather than a punishing chore.

However, my time back also highlighted a persistent, underlying issue: the game feels like it's being developed by a very small team with limited resources. Promised seasonal features often arrive in a bare-bones state. The casino launch is a prime example—a feature that should have been part of the core experience was introduced with only one slot machine game and, astoundingly, no way to convert chips back into in-game currency for a full month. This lack of basic functionality points to a troubling pattern.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 216522421

text:
This lack of basic functionality points to a troubling pattern.

This extends to the game's foundational systems. The decision to remain strictly always-online, despite a player base split by platform and region, makes it difficult to populate race lobbies. The severe monetization is another critical flaw. The grind required to complete the Solar Pass and earn its final-tier car is immense—my own 40 hours of play only reached around Level 43, suggesting a 45-hour commitment per season for the primary reward. This feels designed to push players toward buying a more expensive solar pass option that already includes 20 levels, as well as the recently added real-money currency purchases a feature the developers once promised would never be implemented.

So... like many, I purchased this on account of loving TDU1 & TDU2, and finding it for a massive discount.

To begin with - the game crashes. A lot. Though I may have found the primary cause - transitions to and from cutscenes, with the cutscenes attempting to run at 200 FPS. At the end of missions and when entering buildings, the game was locking up and exiting to desktop, literally every 10 minutes. If you have this problem, search online for the config change to force 60FPS cutscenes.

I'm running it on an i5 13600K, with an RTX 3070. I have to run it medum settings at 1440p, limiting the FPS to 60. FPS often hovers beneath 60, which seems utterly ridiculous. Particularly since the graphics are far from brilliant.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 236187310

text:
Particularly since the graphics are far from brilliant.

Now, gameplay. The driving physics seem fairly good, and are a clear upgrade over TDU2. In fact, the physics feel somewhat better than Forza Horizon. The sound too, is very good. Engine sounds are fantastic.

But aside from that... it just feels... dead. There's none of TDU1/2's character. No police chases. Very few activities. The maps are TINY compared to TDU1/2: part of the appeal of the original games was the fact that you could drive for miles and miles, getting lost, seeing what you discover! None of that here.

KT Racing have continued to work on the game, in spite of major financial difficulties from their owners, Nacon. This is admirable. The devs are TRYING to add functionality that should have been in the game to begin with, and again I commend them for this.

Unfortunately, the performance is far worse than expected. For a title released in 2024, you would assume post-launch updates would have addressed major issues. I can’t speak for how it ran at launch, but in its current state, the game is still laughable.

I’m running a Ryzen 7 3700X, an AMD Radeon 9070 XT, and 32GB of DDR4 RAM. On paper, the game runs fine at 1080p on max settings, maintaining a mostly stable 72 FPS—but that’s where the problems start.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 215701034

text:
Every 5–10 seconds while driving, the framerate randomly tanks from 72 FPS down to 4–5 FPS, with no clear cause. There’s no thermal or power throttling involved, as both my CPU and GPU stay below 55°C. This behavior only occurs in Unreal Engine 5 games, which leads me to believe this title uses a modified version of UE5 rebranded as the KT Engine—but don’t be fooled by the name.

Beyond performance, there are serious loading and visual issues. The map frequently fails to load properly, leaving you stuck in place until it eventually catches up—even when the game is installed on an NVMe SSD. Textures often don’t line up correctly, and in some cases, broken textures float above the road, completely blocking your view.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 215701034

text:
Textures often don’t line up correctly, and in some cases, broken textures float above the road, completely blocking your view. This makes Delivery races unnecessarily frustrating, especially since a single crash can cause you to fail the entire event, which usually can’t be restarted.

Wheel support is another major disappointment. I use a MOZA R3 Racing Wheel, and the preset feels like it was created without testing the actual hardware. Most buttons are mapped incorrectly, forcing you to rebind everything manually. The radial menu doesn’t work at all with the wheel, requiring you to use a mouse just to navigate it. Steering angle settings are also broken—they only function correctly if set to the maximum 1080 degrees both in-game and in the Moza Pit House app. Any other setting results in completely inaccurate steering animations.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 215701034

text:
Any other setting results in completely inaccurate steering animations.

The $50 price tag is completely unjustifiable given the game’s condition. I picked it up for $12 and still feel ripped off. Even at its usual sale price of $20, it’s far too much to ask for a game this broken.

*****UPDATE :

I have been playing Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown for around 50 hours, and I wanted to share my personal experience with the game.

There are things I really enjoyed, but there are also many things that honestly should have been noticed and fixed before release.

Graphics and Optimization

First, let's get this out of the way: graphically, this game is not impressive, and it is not well optimized.

This game was released on September 12, 2024. What is the excuse?
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
What is the excuse?

Games like The Crew Motorfest (2023) and Forza Horizon 5 (2021) look absolutely gorgeous compared to TDUSC.

For a racing game where the main focus is cars and driving, it is disappointing that a game released in late 2024 looks behind titles that came out years before it.

*Cars, Dealerships, and Handling

There are only 14 dealerships across the entire map, containing around 90 cars, plus 7 clan-exclusive cars.

The biggest issue is that many of these cars are simply not enjoyable to drive. I would say around 30% or more feel almost undrivable because of how poorly they handle.

For example, I was really looking forward to buying the Mercedes-Benz SL 65 AMG, but what a disappointment. The handling is terrible, and many people who bought it have complained about it.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
The handling is terrible, and many people who bought it have complained about it.

The same goes for the 1987 Ferrari F40.

One of the most iconic cars ever made somehow drives like garbage in TDUSC. It honestly feels like they added the F40 just to disrespect Ferrari rather than celebrate one of their legendary cars.

The funny thing is, if you want to avoid wasting money, just buy Lamborghinis. They are cheap, fast, handle well, and will win races.

But if you buy cars because you actually like them, you will struggle, especially on higher difficulties. The game basically forces you to use the meta BiS (Best-in-Slot) cars if you want to compete.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
The game basically forces you to use the meta BiS (Best-in-Slot) cars if you want to compete.

*Driving, Racing Line, and Camera Issues

One thing I noticed from games like Forza Horizon and The Crew is how much you can trust your car. Even at high speeds, you understand how the car will react.

TDUSC lacks that feeling. Sometimes you take a corner that should be easy, yet you still end up hitting the wall.

The racing line is another problem. Sometimes it stays cyan, telling you that you should not slow down, but following it sends you into walls or off mountains.

So what is the problem? Is the racing line unreliable, or is the handling not polished enough? Personally, I think it is both.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
Personally, I think it is both.

Crashes in this game are also much more punishing compared to Forza Horizon or The Crew Motorfest. If the game wants clean driving to matter, then the tools it gives you need to be reliable.

Speaking of badly designed things, the camera angles need work.

Sometimes while racing, you genuinely lose sight of the racing line or even the road itself for a full second when going up and down hills. It's honestly frustrating, especially when you're driving at high speeds.

I tried adjusting the camera settings, but nothing seems to solve the issue.

I have been playing racing games since Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2 (2002), and I'm genuinely surprised that an issue like this still exists in a racing game released in 2024.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
The developers simply needed to play their own game for a few hours to notice these problems.

*Race Design and Progression

The game tries hard to encourage clean driving, and I actually like that idea.

However, some races are badly designed. On the Ibiza map, some roads are so narrow that overtaking becomes almost impossible unless you drive dirty.

Some sections feel like they were designed for only one car to fit through.

After reaching Reputation Level 60, the progression also becomes disappointing.

When you start, Every 5 levels, you receive the same message saying a new bulletin is incoming, followed by a low-quality video explaining that new races and cars have unlocked.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
After level 60, you get around 40 extra quests, but most of them are just:

"Finish 100 races in first place with this car."

The reward?

A sticker and 1 million credits.

the endgame feels repetitive and soulless.

*Things I Actually Liked

One thing I really appreciate is that the game does not allow the ridiculous off-roading seen in Forza.

You cannot just drive through forests, take impossible shortcuts, and win races. If you leave the road, you are usually stuck.

Of course, the game has Cross Country races, but those are mostly designed around actual dirt roads, which I think is the correct approach.

The Contract Missions are also a nice addition.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 229734372

text:
The Contract Missions are also a nice addition.

Taxi contracts, car deliveries, and other activities give you something different to do besides racing.

The Taxi missions are especially interesting because some customers want speed, while others require realistic driving: stopping at lights, using indicators, and avoiding crashes.

*Final Thoughts

Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown has a good foundation. The idea behind the game is there: an open world, car collecting, and a focus on driving.

Unfortunately, too many small problems hold it back: poor optimization, inconsistent handling, unreliable racing lines, weak progression, and a LACK OF POLISH.

Most of these issues are things the developers should have noticed themselves by simply playing the game.

The potential was there, but the game needed more time, testing, and attention to detail before release.

Road variety. Different road types actually feel distinct to drive on, not just visually different skins on the same physics.
Traffic behavior. Traffic density drops during off-peak hours like it would in real life, and AI cars actually change lanes to avoid congestion instead of just sitting there. Small touch, but it makes the world feel alive.

text:
TL;DR If you come into this game with tempered expectations (and a heavily discounted price), and don't mind some rough edges, I think there's definitely some enjoyment to be had, especially if you're a car nut.

If you've played any of the previous Test Drive Unlimited games, you'll be right at home here. It definitely takes a lot more after the second game, given the premise once again revolves around rich people bank rolling a racing tournament.

The structure hasn't changed much either, start in the lower powered cars and work your way up to the super and hyper cars.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 222443790

text:
However, the cars you have access to are restricted by level, and levelling is a bit grindy, at 17 hours of playtime I've only just reached level 30 which grants access to super cars, hyper cars are locked at level 50. Though you don't just have to grind races, the side missions of acting as a taxi, delivery driver and tailing missions also returned from TDU2. The taxi missions in particular have had some big changes, with there now being multiple passenger types, some who require you to obey traffic laws, others driving smoothly etc.

The driving itself feels pretty good, given KT Racing's history with the WRC games, they do know how to make a decent driving engine (pun intended), and if you've played any of the WRC games you might feel some of the handling here.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 222443790

text:
By no means is it a simulation, cars are still very loose and easy to slide, but you do understeer in the wet and good driving technique will be required for the technical tracks.

Visually I'd say it's a mixed bag and it changes heavily based on the environment. The car models clearly had the bulk of the resources put into them, and in the right lighting they can look great. The setting of Hong Kong looks well realised and both the urban and countryside areas are detailed enough for a racing game, though you'll definitely notice plenty of copy & pasted assets. The rain effects look great, especially in the cockpit view.
title: Test Drive Unlimited Solar Crown — review 222443790

text:
The avatar and human models drew the short straw in the resource department, they don't look much better than the ones in TDU2, with weird shaders on the skin. One major gripe I have is the lack of proper anti-aliasing support, it only supports FXAA or TXAA.

In terms of performance it runs okay on my machine with a Ryzen 12 core and RX 7900XTX, getting about 90 fps running at 1440p, with some dips in areas with a lot of trees.

There's also a microtransaction economy, but I'm choosing to ignore it, there's nothing there that would make the game Pay to Win, though if you do want some of the cars that are offered by it, they're not cheap and you only get very small amounts of the premium currency given to you. This game does the same thing a number of other games do, like Dead Island or Dying Light or Far Cry, but with one crucial difference, which is that there is ABSOLUTELY NO ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. So often I get into an open world shooter like this and find myself losing endless time to things that are neither looting nor shooting: long, dull cutscenes; unnecessary travel time across unnecessarily oversized and empty maps; horribly designed mini-games and side activities. None of it is ever fun, just terrible padding. This game does not have that problem. You explore, you shoot, and you loot. And it's very good at all of those things.

The hallmarks of Arkane are definitely still here. You can approach fights strategically, using positioning and environmental hazards. World building and design are absolutely top notch (I will say there's significantly less story than in something like Dishonored or Prey, but what there is is very well done, I think). text: Redfall, developed by Arkane Austin and published by Bethesda Softworks, is a game built on a premise that should have been a genre standout: an open-world vampire shooter set in a mist-covered Massachusetts island town cut off from the rest of the world. The sun has been blotted out, the tides have frozen in place, and supernatural predators stalk abandoned streets. As one of four survivors — each with their own powers and personality — you set out to unravel the mystery behind the town’s downfall and push back against the vampiric forces tightening their grip. On paper, it reads like a compelling combination of Arkane’s atmospheric storytelling and a more action-oriented co-op shooter structure. And in its earliest moments, Redfall occasionally hints at what that game could have been.
title: Redfall — review 212739989

text:
And in its earliest moments, Redfall occasionally hints at what that game could have been.

The four playable heroes offer a nice conceptual variety: a telekinetic student, a gadget-driven inventor, a marksman with a spectral companion, and a cryptozoologist with arcane abilities. Their powers complement one another well in theory, creating opportunities for synergy in co-op play and allowing different approaches in solo runs. The town of Redfall itself also has a strong sense of identity. Quaint colonial houses, eerie farmland, vampire-controlled safehouses, cultist-infested streets, and unnervingly quiet waterfronts set the stage for encounters that combine looter-shooter mechanics with occasional touches of supernatural horror. At its rare best, the game achieves small moments of tension—creeping into a flickering house while listening for whispers, or stumbling across a vampire nest that warps local reality.
title: Redfall — review 212739989

text:
Combat follows familiar first-person shooter rhythms blended with light RPG elements. Weapons come in tiers, each offering bonuses or traits, and vampires must be weakened before a stake, UV blast, or fire finishes them off. Abilities provide extra mobility, defensive tools, or offensive surges. When players coordinate these tools successfully, fights can feel energetic and chaotic in a fun way. The game supports full co-op, and playing with friends unquestionably improves the pacing by adding layers of strategy and broader firepower. Even basic enemy encounters become more dynamic when teamwork enters the equation.

But while Redfall’s foundations are structurally sound, the execution frequently struggles to match the ambition. One of its most persistent issues is the emptiness of the open world.
title: Redfall — review 212739989

text:
One of its most persistent issues is the emptiness of the open world. Despite the atmospheric setting, large sections of the map feel devoid of life, interactivity, or meaningful encounters. Many buildings exist as hollow set pieces, and stretches of the town have little to do beyond moving from objective to objective. What should feel like a breathing, terrified community instead comes across as static and underpopulated, weakening the immersion and removing much of the tension a vampire takeover should evoke.

Enemy behavior also contributes to this lack of engagement. Human cultists and vampire foes alike often display rudimentary or erratic AI, which diminishes both challenge and atmosphere. Rather than stalking, flanking, or overwhelming players in clever ways, many enemies simply run forward or stand in place, making combat too predictable.
title: Redfall — review 212739989

text:
The game introduces elite vampire types, but their rarity — combined with the flatness of ordinary encounters — reduces the stakes that should define a supernatural shooter. As players advance, especially with powerful loot, the combat loop begins to lose urgency and variety.

Narratively, Redfall never fully capitalizes on its intriguing setup. Much of the story is conveyed through static images and exposition rather than dynamic sequences or environmental storytelling of the kind Arkane is known for. The central villains — the so-called Vampire Gods — are conceptually fascinating but underdeveloped, leaving major threads feeling unresolved or detached. Even the heroes, though distinct in personality, rarely interact meaningfully during missions, which becomes especially noticeable in co-op. As a result, the story feels more like a loose framework for missions than a driving emotional arc.
title: Redfall — review 212739989

text:
As a result, the story feels more like a loose framework for missions than a driving emotional arc.

Technical issues further complicate the experience. At launch and even beyond, players encountered inconsistent performance, odd animations, texture pop-in, hit detection quirks, and a general lack of polish. While patches have improved some aspects, the impression remains that the game arrived in an unfinished state. These problems don’t make Redfall unplayable, but they exacerbate its already uneven pacing and presentation.

Co-op progression design is another misstep. Only the host of a session receives full campaign progression, meaning friends who join must replay missions again later if they want credit in their own worlds. This choice undermines the cooperative fantasy the game heavily advertises and discourages spontaneous drop-in play. Combined with the lack of enemy scaling tuned for groups, co-op can alternate between being trivially easy and oddly chaotic.

Combined with the lack of enemy scaling tuned for groups, co-op can alternate between being trivially easy and oddly chaotic.

In the end, Redfall is a game full of potential that flickers intermittently but never fully ignites. There are fragments of an atmospheric supernatural shooter scattered throughout its world — an abandoned house filled with cult paraphernalia, a silent lighthouse overlooking a blood-red sea, a tense fight inside a warped vampire nest — but these moments are isolated rather than foundational. The overall experience feels stretched thin, with world design, AI, narrative depth, and technical performance all falling short of the ambitions driving the project.

Players who enjoy light looter-shooter mechanics, casual co-op play, or simply exploring eerie environments with friends may still find pockets of enjoyment. But those seeking a polished, narratively rich, or mechanically sharp experience — especially given Arkane’s pedigree — may walk away disappointed.

This is the first Arkane game that I don't enjoy.

Despite the difference in genre from most Arkane titles, I was excited. The trailers made this game look fun. Despite the difference in genre, I'd like to point to how good Prey 2017 was (despite the low sales and poor ending) and what could have been for Arkane Austin's Redfall...

Redfall's open world is empty, and the enemies that populate it are hilariously dumb. Let me touch on both:

I think a good way to describe the open world is with an example. On the north-east side of town, there's a house you can actually enter. It's a normal house, furnished although a large amount of empty space in it.

text:
It's a normal house, furnished although a large amount of empty space in it. In the backyard, there's a large shed that you can also enter. For about 50 meters around the shed, there is nothing but flat, freshly cut grass. No bushes, flowers, nothing. And inside this large shed? Nothing. An empty, fully textured shed with a pool leaning up against the wall.
The world feels like it's too big for itself, and yet in 3 hours I had been around half of the whole town. I noticed that a truck with cultists had spawned and the disappeared later on, meaning that the empty space is supposed to be filled with things that can change. Now I was also thinking "oh it's an Arkane game, they're meant to be dumb so that I can find fun ways to kill them!" There are so few ways to go about doing that: guns, and your abilities that do pitiful amounts of damage. text:
Anywhere I wasn't looking, in the heat of battle, enemies would spawn in a room I had just cleared. I actually saw them spawn at one point. Maybe I had whipped around too fast or something?

Despite being a different Arkane studio, it's worth making the comparison. DEATHLOOP, despite it's arguably worse optimisation, is a better game. It even shares some of the same RPG gimmicks as Redfall. I wanted to love Redfall, and I want Arkane to prove me wrong and make me buy this again in the future once they do something with it. A Vampire Game That Sucks… But Not in a Good Way

I went into Redfall hoping for at least a decent co-op shooter, but what I got instead was one of the most shockingly bad AAA releases in recent years. This game is an absolute disaster on almost every level, and the negative reviews are 100% deserved.

It's dark, and you get a real feeling of accomplishment as you take down each member of the group.
You have a hub in both sections of the game; Redfall and Burial Point, with survivors who have their own stories and side missions you can complete. text:
PROs:

✅ Rich with lore through numerous notes and readable items.
✅ Great potential for co-op shenanigans.
✅ Solid variety of skills and weapons.
✅ Distinctive and well-executed artistic style.
✅ Good original soundtrack.

CONs:

❌ Excessive junk loot with little to no purpose.
❌ The co-op is completely broken on the second map, making the game impossible to finish.
❌ The world feels empty and inconsistent in many areas.
❌ Characters are visually unappealing and bland, with what feels like forced diversity.
❌ Numerous game-breaking bugs in co-op that require restarting the session.
❌ The weapon affix system quickly becomes stale, removing the excitement of finding cool new items.
❌ Poor enemy AI.

Comments:

Honestly, this game had some rather solid ideas and a promising combination of genres. A big kudos to the writers who fleshed out the world with plenty of lore. The game also ran smoothly, and the combat, for the most part, felt satisfying.

Unfortunately, the game is hampered by too many "unfinished" and "bare minimum" features that make the overall experience lackluster.

We were unable to finish the game because the co-op on the second map is completely broken. After a certain point, we were met with a permanent loading screen. Redfall – A Second Chance Worth Taking

I recently reinstalled Redfall after shelving it shortly after launch, and honestly? I’m impressed. This game had a rough start—no denying that. At release, it was plagued with performance issues, lackluster AI, and just felt unfinished. Like many, I dropped it with a sense of disappointment. But curiosity got the better of me, and after hearing about a string of updates, I gave it another shot.

I’m glad I did.

After diving back in, I spent around four hours exploring the vampire-infested world of Redfall, both solo and in online co-op with friends—and I can confidently say the experience is so much smoother now. The combat feels sharp and responsive, movement is fluid, and best of all, I didn’t encounter a single crash or noticeable bug. Lag? Gone. Enemies? Actually engaging. The improvements are real.

Resident Evil Resistance is an asymmetrical multiplayer survival horror game developed by Capcom. It was released as the online component bundled with *Resident Evil 3*, offering a unique 4v1 gameplay experience.

In each match, four survivors must work together to escape while a fifth player takes on the role of the “Mastermind,” controlling traps, zombies, and bioweapons to stop them. This setup creates a constant battle between teamwork and strategy.

The core gameplay is fun and chaotic. Survivors need to cooperate—managing resources, solving small objectives, and fighting off enemies—while the Mastermind strategically places threats and controls powerful creatures like Mr. X. Matches can feel intense, especially when both sides are experienced.

Another downside is the lack of long-term content and updates, which caused the game to lose popularity over time.

Overall, **Resident Evil Resistance** is an interesting multiplayer experiment with fun ideas, but it lacks the polish and support needed to keep players engaged long-term.

text:
Honestly, I liked this game a lot when I first started playing it. The idea of a 4v1 multiplayer game set in the Resident Evil universe was genuinely fun, and there were plenty of matches where everything just clicked. Escaping as a survivor felt rewarding, and playing as the Mastermind could be surprisingly entertaining too. It wasn't perfect, but it had enough unique ideas that I kept coming back to it for quite a while.

The biggest strength of the game was its potential. Every character had their own role, matches could play out very differently, and there was a good amount of tension when both sides were evenly matched. When everyone was actually playing the game normally, it could be a really fun experience. It felt different from a lot of other asymmetrical multiplayer games out there.
title: Resident Evil Resistance — review 227546225

text:
It felt different from a lot of other asymmetrical multiplayer games out there.

Unfortunately, the longer I played, the more the problems started showing up. The biggest one by far was hackers and exploiters. There were too many matches where something felt off, whether it was suspicious players, weird lag, or mechanics being abused in ways that clearly weren't intended. After a while it became difficult to tell if you lost because the other side played better or because something else was going on. That slowly killed my motivation to keep playing.

The peer-to-peer connection system didn't help either. Some matches ran fine, while others felt like a complete mess. Combined with the lack of proper anti-cheat measures, it made the experience feel less reliable than it should have been. It's a shame because underneath all those issues was a genuinely enjoyable game.

This is the Resident Evil game I played after completing the entire franchise up to RE Village, and it is a multiplayer title with an interesting concept that can be engaging depending on the situation. The main challenge on PC is finding enough players to start matches, but once that issue is resolved, it runs fairly well. The gameplay loop is fast and rewarding once the systems are understood. The mechanics are simple to learn, and the design and atmosphere are well crafted. There are also mods that add extra variety and depth to the overall experience.

There is a noticeable learning curve at the beginning, especially when trying to gain better equipment. Progress can feel slow at first, and saving credits for the higher-tier packs is the most effective way to advance. Once stronger options are unlocked, matches become more balanced and flow more smoothly.

When I bought Resident Evil 3, I was hyped because it came with a “free” copy of Resident Evil Resistance.

text:
A Broken Multiplayer Experience

Experience a new 1 vs 4 online multiplayer game set in the Resident Evil universe where four survivors face-off against a sinister Mastermind.

Story

In September 1998, during the Raccoon City outbreak, Umbrella Corporation abducted civilians and brought them to the “NEST2” facility. There, employees deliberately infected them to test and demonstrate the effectiveness of the T-Virus Project.

Gameplay

Resistance's gameplay is similar to Resident Evil Outbreak (2003). Resident Evil: Resistance is a third-person, asymmetrical multiplayer mode where four Survivors go up against one Mastermind. Each Survivor has their own special abilities, and they must work together to solve puzzles, activate terminals, and complete objectives before time runs out. Teamwork is key—you need to revive teammates, share supplies, and push through waves of traps and monsters to survive.

text:
Teamwork is key—you need to revive teammates, share supplies, and push through waves of traps and monsters to survive.

The Mastermind plays from a completely different perspective, watching everything through security cameras. You can set traps, spawn enemies and bioweapons, and even take direct control of monsters. Using a deck of hazard cards, you can constantly manipulate the environment to block, delay, or destroy the Survivors’ progress.

Enemies & Bosses

The same enemies and bosses from both Resident Evil 2 and 3.

Environment

There are seven levels: Downtown, Uptown, Casino, Prison, Research Facility, Abandoned Park and Bemusement Park. The environment is simple but full of traps and enemies created by the Mastermind. You have an automap as the survivors, showing you the locations of teammates and objectives.

Same as the base game.

text:

Constructive Criticism

Unfortunately, this game struggles with a few balance and technical issues. The Survivor vs. Mastermind setup can often feel uneven, with one side having a clear advantage depending on the players or match conditions.

On top of that, the game’s technical performance can be hit-or-miss. Because it doesn’t use dedicated servers, it relies on peer-to-peer connections, which can lead to lag, stuttering, and inconsistent gameplay—especially when the Mastermind is hosting the match.

There are also concerns about content and replay value. It lacks depth and variety, making it feel more like a bonus mode or experiment rather than a full-fledged multiplayer experience. The game is also very dead and full of bugs and cheaters.
title: Resident Evil Resistance — review 209128528

text:
The game is also very dead and full of bugs and cheaters.

The UI for Survivors is horrible. The HUD is too big, especially the map that covers half the screen.

The Verdict

Overall, Resident Evil: Resistance offers an interesting concept that blends strategy, cooperation, and survival horror, putting a fresh spin on the classic Resident Evil formula. The cat-and-mouse gameplay between Survivors and the Mastermind can be tense and exciting—especially when taking control of iconic series bosses as the Mastermind.

However, the fun quickly fades. Beneath the promising idea lies an experience that feels unfinished and poorly maintained. Persistent lag, network instability, and the absence of dedicated servers lead to frustrating, inconsistent matches. Over time, the game has also become plagued by cheaters and bugs, making it virtually unplayable in 2025.

Resident Evil Resistance is a fascinating experiment that brings a fun, arcade-style multiplayer spin to the universe. Pitting a team of four Survivors against a Mastermind who controls the map in real-time, it creates a gripping cat-and-mouse dynamic.

Playing as the Survivors requires tight teamwork, smart resource management, and quick escape tactics as you race against a shrinking clock. On the flip side, playing as the Mastermind—spawning zombies, setting up traps, locking doors, and eventually taking direct control of iconic tyrants like Mr. X or Nemesis—is deliciously evil and immensely satisfying.

text: RESIDENT EVIL RESISTANCE attempts an ambitious 4v1 asymmetrical multiplayer concept that pits a team of four cooperative survivors against a single, tactical Mastermind. The core mechanical hook blends traditional third-person survival horror action with real-time strategic management, requiring survivors to complete time-based puzzle objectives while the opponent spawns creatures and traps via security cameras. Visually, the title utilizes the RE Engine to deliver atmospheric, asset-dense testing chambers and fluid character animations that align well with the franchise's modern aesthetic. This structural duality provides a genuinely unique concept that promises high-stakes tension and distinct, varied playstyles for both factions.
title: Resident Evil Resistance — review 227812879

text:
This structural duality provides a genuinely unique concept that promises high-stakes tension and distinct, varied playstyles for both factions.

However, severe balancing issues and critical technical limitations fundamentally undermine the overall experience, turning matches into repetitive exercises in frustration. High-level Mastermind strategies frequently utilize oppressive, stun-locking trap combinations that leave survivors with minimal counter-play, while the lack of dedicated servers results in severe, match-disrupting peer-to-peer latency. Because the title was bundled exclusively with a shortened mainline campaign rather than receiving standalone polish, the gameplay loop suffers from a lack of long-term developer support and inadequate anti-cheat measures. Ultimately, the software fails to sustain its intriguing premise, resulting in a deeply flawed execution that remains an underwhelming and largely abandoned addition to the franchise's multiplayer portfolio.

text: The level scaling is ROUGH, for starters. You don't really feel like you're making any impact at all until you get a character to around level 7-10, which is about 4 hours of gameplay. It also matches you with max-ranked players incredibly frequently, regardless of whether or not you're playing mastermind or survivor; because the gear and skills scale so hard up to level 25, you will constantly be getting wrecked. An example is playing an L3 Annette (the first mastermind you can play) with only +8% to creature damage, while a L25 Becca is using a build that gives her literally +230% damage (we've done the math), and can kill your toughest creature in 0.5s.

The inverse is also true, Sam is a pretty broken character right now after level 11, but before that a max rank Daniel mastermind controlling a zombie can *literally* 2-shot you (he has a build that can 1-shot all but 2 characters).

The game is time based, so all gameplay is rush-rush-rush; new players are often left in the dust by their team just trying to figure out where they need to go, and smart masterminds punish that mistake *heavily*, causing you to throw the match by simply not knowing the map.

text:
Resident Evil Resistance Review

There are tons of fun to be had, but it could be better!

Some key points that this game offers:

1. 1 vs 4
2. Character Builds
3. Procedural item placement

Gameplay & Controls:

Resident Evil 3 Remake lacks a New Game Plus mode, which was deeply disappointing. Personally, that was the one Remake I was truly looking forward to. To make up for that we have Resident Evil Resistance.

It’s a 4 vs 1 online multiplayer game with one game mode. 4 Survivors have to work together to escape from the 1, the Mastermind. As Survivors, you need to work together to keep each other alive whilst you work together finding a means of escape.
title: Resident Evil Resistance — review 90898989

text:
To prevent your escape the Mastermind will lock doors and place nasty surprises around every nook and corner to prevent you from escaping. These range from a variety of Zombie and other BOW types, to traps and other devious tricks.
There are several different Masterminds to choose from, all popular RE villains such as Annette Birkin, Alex Wesker, and Ozwell Spencer himself! Each of them has its own unique skills and abilities. The Survivors are all a bunch of random strangers that have to band together to survive. We have several different survivors, each with their own unique abilities and skills. Adding to their capabilities, each Survivor represents a class; January Van Sant being a hacker, for example, that can take down the camera’s the Mastermind uses to deter the survivor’s progress.
title: Resident Evil Resistance — review 90898989

text:
Even though there are limited maps to play on, no map is ever the same. Key items are always randomly placed so it is always a search and go for these items to progress. Valerie Harmon is a key survivor to have in every match. Not only is she a healer but her ability to scan the environment for key items and resources are key to victory. She is a must have character, because the game lacks a mini-map so her ability to scan the surrounding area really is a lifesaver.

Playing as another survivor does make the lack of a mini-map feel like a nuisance but the lacking adds to the challenge and immersion. Survivor combat is rather effective but unbalanced at times. Some actions feel way too underpowered with others feeling overpowered again.

Graphics:

The game is more than just beautiful. The character models were created remarkably well. Each survivor has their own unique appearance and personality. Enemy models were given the same treatment. Whether it's our regular favourite Zombies or those nasty Lickers, they all look remarkably well designed. Level design is gorgeous! Every corridor, room, and hallway has been cleverly designed to be a battleground, or struggle for survival.

The only issue I have with the graphics is weapons fire, every now and then weapons fire will give you this feedback that makes it seem like the bullet never hit the target.

text:
Sounds:

Voice over artists did a decent job with their scripts. Adding witty comments or creepy gestures as you struggle to escape or kill your experiments…

The music complements the game's tension and atmosphere magnificently.

Replayability:

As you play and complete matches, you are rewarded with RP; this is used again to buy new gear to help you in your future fights. You also rank up with the Survivor/ Mastermind you play as, and as they rank up, they unlock new skills.

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers Ahead:

RE Resistance gives you a lot of Dead by Daylight vibes, essentially it is similar in concept. The gameplay is fun and entertaining, but it runs dry very quickly. Playing as the Mastermind is the real fun here. You have more control and the mission parameters are so much more unique and fun.

text: Spacebase DF-9 is a colony management simulation developed by Double Fine Productions and published by Double Fine Productions, later distributed on Steam under Xbox Game Studios. Set in a distant future where humanity has spread across the stars, the game casts players as the administrator of an isolated space station tasked with housing settlers, managing resources, and surviving the countless dangers of life in deep space. Its concept is immediately appealing: build a thriving orbital community from a handful of rooms and personnel, then watch as its inhabitants create stories of friendship, tragedy, and survival. Even years after its release, the title remains an intriguing example of a game built on an exceptional premise.

text:
Even years after its release, the title remains an intriguing example of a game built on an exceptional premise.

The gameplay centers on constructing and maintaining a space station piece by piece. Players begin with a modest outpost and gradually expand it into a bustling habitat complete with sleeping quarters, recreational areas, infirmaries, security offices, and industrial facilities. Oxygen management, power distribution, and resource collection are constant concerns, ensuring that every expansion carries risks alongside rewards. Nearby asteroids can be mined for valuable materials, while abandoned ships drifting through space provide opportunities for scavenging. These mechanics create a satisfying loop of exploration, construction, and maintenance that encourages players to think several steps ahead.

One of Spacebase DF-9's greatest strengths is its ability to generate memorable scenarios through its simulation systems.

text:
One of Spacebase DF-9's greatest strengths is its ability to generate memorable scenarios through its simulation systems. Colonists develop personalities and react to the environment around them, creating moments that feel surprisingly personal. A station may operate smoothly for hours before an unexpected meteor strike breaches a critical corridor, causing a chain reaction of panic and decompression. Hostile intruders, alien infestations, and equipment failures add further unpredictability, transforming ordinary management tasks into desperate attempts to save the colony. The game's dark humor shines throughout these moments, giving even catastrophic failures an oddly entertaining quality.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and colorful presentation that makes managing a growing station relatively easy. Individual characters are simple in design but expressive enough to convey their actions and emotions.

text:
Watching crews move between departments and interact with one another adds life to the station, while the ambient soundtrack reinforces the feeling of being stranded in an endless expanse of space. The user interface is straightforward, allowing players to focus on building and responding to emergencies without becoming overwhelmed by excessive complexity.

Unfortunately, Spacebase DF-9 is equally known for its unrealized potential. Originally released through Early Access, the game generated considerable excitement due to its ambitious roadmap and the reputation of its developer. However, many of the promised systems never reached completion, leaving the final release feeling smaller in scope than players expected. Certain mechanics lack depth, and progression eventually reveals limitations in artificial intelligence and station management. Rather than evolving into a definitive colony simulator, the game often feels like a snapshot of a much larger vision that never fully came together.

This getting started kicks off the game and it will scare people away.

On paper, interesting things do happen. Derelict space stations will come into your area for you to explore and spaceships will dock with you. From there you have a choice, send your security over to investigate them or ignore them. The spaceships become part of your base where then you need to claim each room, which can be tedious and cumbersome since many small rooms are just tough to click on.

People can come aboard infected with a disease and then your science station will be put to work finding the cure. To do so, click whatever science room you've setup and select whatever they should research. There are a number of diseases to cure and upgrades to unlock. Upgrades include things like body armor and heavier doors.
title: Spacebase DF-9 — review 20260268

text:
Upgrades include things like body armor and heavier doors.

You will get attacked from time to time. Raiders will float out in space and either try to shoot your miners as they pass by or they will board your station. Other times vessels will dock with your station and you'll be invaded. The catch is, unless you're watching a mining operation, its easy to spot and prepare for. You can have your security waiting for them, unless they're busy putting out a fire. It seems like more of an annoyance than a fun or cool challenge. You can also purchase wall mounted defense turrets.

Normal crew will still engage the enemy if they're in the same room, but to send crew in to fight hostiles, you'll need to assign crew to the security.
title: Spacebase DF-9 — review 20260268

text:
Normal crew will still engage the enemy if they're in the same room, but to send crew in to fight hostiles, you'll need to assign crew to the security. From there you can make a security beacon that draws them to the area. It feels like an extra step and even marking the point and calling off security seems like it could be streamlined. A lot of the game needs to be streamlined.

Once attackers are incapacitated you can act to cuff, uncuff or execute them. In fact you can chose to execute or cuff any of your crew. Its just a little odd. Sometimes they will even chose to join your crew. Once resources become scarce, its just easier to execute them and dump them into the refiners to make matter.
title: Spacebase DF-9 — review 20260268

text:
Once resources become scarce, its just easier to execute them and dump them into the refiners to make matter.

Sometimes there is an issue where a firefight in an airlock can down the only crew inside the station. So anyone outside the station is forced to suffocate over time because the air lock refuses to open when someone is in there without a suit. It gets more hilarious because in smaller stations, crew will just stand in the air lock when its too crowded everywhere else. Spacebase DF-9 is an amazing game to watch because of its logic.

Speaking of logic, I managed to glitch the game into thinking there was no airlock. Those outside the station would die of asphyxiation and those inside the station would stay in there. Even crew joining would stay outside until they died.

text:

text: RollerCoaster Tycoon World, developed by Nvizzio Creations and published by Atari and RCTO Productions, was meant to be the triumphant return of one of the most beloved simulation franchises in gaming history. Carrying the iconic RollerCoaster Tycoon name, it set out to deliver a modernized version of the classic theme park-building experience that had captivated players for decades. The promise was enticing: a full 3D world, advanced coaster-building tools, robust park management systems, and seamless Steam Workshop integration for sharing custom content. However, upon release in late 2016, the game quickly became one of the most controversial entries in the series, remembered more for its missteps than for its innovations. What was intended to be a revival of a legendary brand instead became a cautionary tale about the dangers of mismatched expectations and rushed execution.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text: At its core, RollerCoaster Tycoon World adheres to the familiar formula that defines the franchise. Players are tasked with designing, building, and managing a thriving amusement park from the ground up. You create pathways, place attractions, manage finances, monitor guest happiness, and, of course, design the roller coasters that form the centerpiece of your park. Nvizzio introduced a new spline-based coaster construction system, which was a major departure from the traditional segment-based track building of earlier games. This system allows for smoother, more organic track layouts, enabling players to craft intricate designs with loops, twists, and banking curves that flow more naturally than in previous iterations. The physics engine, though imperfect, was designed to simulate realistic coaster movement, complete with the potential for derailments if designs were poorly executed.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
Riding your own creations in first-person was one of the game’s genuine highlights, offering a sense of thrill and satisfaction that recalled the wonder of classic RollerCoaster Tycoon moments.

On paper, the game’s feature list was impressive. Beyond coaster construction, RollerCoaster Tycoon World introduced full 3D park environments with terrain manipulation, dynamic lighting, and the “Park Pulse” system—a data-driven overview of guest feedback and park performance. It also embraced modern community features, integrating Steam Workshop to allow players to share custom rides, structures, and entire parks. The inclusion of modding tools seemed to indicate a desire to nurture a creative and collaborative player base. The sandbox mode, meanwhile, offered freedom from financial restrictions and allowed for pure creative experimentation. It was, in concept, the perfect evolution of the franchise: a simulation that honored its roots while expanding its scope with modern technology and user-generated content.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
It was, in concept, the perfect evolution of the franchise: a simulation that honored its roots while expanding its scope with modern technology and user-generated content.

Unfortunately, the final product failed to deliver on much of its potential. From the moment of its release, RollerCoaster Tycoon World was plagued by technical problems, performance instability, and an overall lack of polish. Even on powerful systems, the game suffered from frame drops, long load times, and erratic simulation behavior. The interface felt cumbersome, often requiring too many clicks for basic tasks, and the management tools lacked the depth and precision that fans expected. Guest AI was particularly disappointing—visitors would wander aimlessly, ignore amenities, or behave in illogical ways, breaking the illusion of a living, breathing park. The Park Pulse system, while ambitious, ended up feeling disconnected from gameplay, presenting data without meaningful ways to act on it.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
The visual presentation, though bright and colorful, lacked personality. Compared to the crisp, stylized charm of earlier Tycoon games or the detailed realism of its contemporaries, it felt flat and unrefined.

Perhaps the most frustrating aspect of RollerCoaster Tycoon World is how close it came to being something great. The new coaster-building system, despite its quirks, is easily the most enjoyable part of the experience. Crafting elaborate designs and then testing them in first-person mode provides genuine excitement, and moments of creativity shine through even amidst the game’s flaws. However, that enjoyment is often undermined by broken physics, buggy terrain collisions, and restrictive building tools. Queue paths frequently snap into awkward configurations, ride entrances and exits are rigidly placed, and attempts to fine-tune layouts often result in unpredictable errors.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
The game offers glimpses of fun—moments when your park hums with life and coasters roar across the skyline—but these moments are fleeting, buried beneath layers of frustration and instability.

In terms of management simulation, RollerCoaster Tycoon World also falls short of its predecessors. Financial systems, staff management, and guest needs are simplified to the point of redundancy. Staffing mechanics lack meaningful control, and balancing budgets rarely requires strategic thought. The simulation often feels hollow, as though the numbers are merely cosmetic rather than representing a dynamic system. This is particularly disappointing given how the original RollerCoaster Tycoon titles thrived on the intricate interplay between design and management. Here, the player’s decisions rarely feel impactful, and the park’s success seems to depend more on patience with the game’s quirks than on true managerial skill.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
Here, the player’s decisions rarely feel impactful, and the park’s success seems to depend more on patience with the game’s quirks than on true managerial skill.

A major factor that compounded the game’s failure was its timing. Released within days of Frontier Developments’ Planet Coaster, RollerCoaster Tycoon World immediately suffered from unfavorable comparisons. Planet Coaster not only delivered the kind of modernized experience fans had hoped for—it exceeded expectations with its deep creative tools, intuitive controls, and polished presentation. RollerCoaster Tycoon World, by contrast, felt dated and incomplete upon arrival. Many players accused Atari of rushing it to market to compete directly with Frontier, resulting in a game that simply wasn’t ready. The backlash was swift and severe, with reviews criticizing its bugs, shallow systems, and disappointing visuals. Even years later, community sentiment remains largely negative, with most fans recommending the older titles or Planet Coaster as superior alternatives.

text:
Even years later, community sentiment remains largely negative, with most fans recommending the older titles or Planet Coaster as superior alternatives.

Despite its troubled legacy, there are players who find enjoyment in RollerCoaster Tycoon World’s sandbox mode. When stripped of objectives and allowed to build freely, the game can still provide moments of creativity and relaxation. The Steam Workshop community, while smaller than that of its competitors, has also produced custom content that helps alleviate some of the base game’s shortcomings. For those with patience and lowered expectations, there is still a certain nostalgic pleasure to be found in creating coasters, watching crowds gather, and listening to the familiar hum of amusement park chaos. But these moments are fleeting reminders of what could have been—a testament to the enduring appeal of the RollerCoaster Tycoon concept even in imperfect form.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 206400531

text:
Ultimately, RollerCoaster Tycoon World is a case study in ambition undermined by poor execution. It had all the right ingredients to reignite the series’ glory: a beloved brand, modern tools, and a passionate fanbase ready to embrace it. But technical flaws, shallow design, and a lack of cohesive vision prevented it from living up to its potential. While it may hold some nostalgic curiosity for diehard fans or those seeking a creative sandbox experience, it falls far short of the standards set by both its predecessors and its competitors. For many, it represents not just a disappointing sequel, but the symbolic end of an era for the RollerCoaster Tycoon franchise—a once-revolutionary series that lost its way trying to find a place in the modern gaming landscape.

It was not worth the early access price I paid ($65). Be ready for bugs and crashes, long loading screans, easily-confused NPCs (peeps), pathing jank, weird coaster-building mechanics, menus that don't sort correctly, and other un-intuitive gameplay elements.

I do however, like the way you can surround Generic (that's what they're called in-game) Rides with themed scenery, and the ride will then count as that other theme in the info window.

Title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World - A Bumpy Ride

RollerCoaster Tycoon World promised to be the next great installment in a beloved franchise, but unfortunately, it falls short of the high expectations set by its predecessors. As a long-time fan of the series, I couldn't help but feel disappointed by the overall experience this game offers.

First and foremost, the graphics and visuals in RollerCoaster Tycoon World are a mixed bag. While the game does offer some impressive coaster designs and colorful attractions, the overall graphical quality feels dated and fails to take advantage of modern gaming hardware. It lacks the polish and attention to detail that one would expect from a game released in the era of advanced graphics.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 146562272

text:
It lacks the polish and attention to detail that one would expect from a game released in the era of advanced graphics.

The gameplay also leaves much to be desired. The game's user interface is clunky and unintuitive, making it a chore to build and manage your theme park efficiently. The AI of park guests and staff can be frustratingly erratic, with visitors frequently getting stuck or behaving in bizarre ways. This can lead to a frustrating experience as you struggle to maintain a smoothly running park.

The coaster-building mechanics, which should be the highlight of any RollerCoaster Tycoon game, are disappointingly limited and lack the depth and creativity seen in earlier titles. Customization options for rides and scenery items are also lacking, which hampers the player's ability to create a truly unique and immersive park.
title: RollerCoaster Tycoon World — review 146562272

text:
Customization options for rides and scenery items are also lacking, which hampers the player's ability to create a truly unique and immersive park.

Multiplayer was touted as a significant feature of RollerCoaster Tycoon World, but it feels like an afterthought rather than a well-integrated gameplay element. The online features are riddled with bugs and connectivity issues, making it difficult to enjoy the game with friends.

On a positive note, RollerCoaster Tycoon World does include Steam Workshop support, allowing the community to create and share custom content. This does add some much-needed replay value to the game, as the base content can quickly become repetitive.

In conclusion, RollerCoaster Tycoon World is a lackluster addition to a beloved franchise. It fails to capture the magic of its predecessors, offering subpar graphics, frustrating gameplay, and a lack of depth.

Payday 3 isn't a terrible game. It introduces some genuinely good ideas and improves parts of the formula, but it often feels like it was developed by a team that didn't fully understand what made Payday so memorable.

What Payday 3 Got Right

Maskless Stealth

Being able to complete parts of a heist without putting on your mask is an excellent addition. Moving Cameras

Security cameras are no longer fixed in place. They now rotate and cover different areas, creating more opportunities to move through blind spots if you're patient enough.

More Natural Guards

One of the biggest frustrations with Payday 2 stealth was how guards seemed to have eyes in the back of their heads. In Payday 3, they behave much more naturally, detecting you only when they actually have line of sight. This makes stealth significantly less frustrating.

In Payday 2, Perk Decks completely transformed how you approached the game.

Crew Chief focused on supporting the entire team by increasing health, damage absorption and stamina.

Grinder and Stoic encouraged health-based builds, working especially well alongside skills like Hostage Taker.

Anarchist and Armorer focused on armor while synergizing with Berserker, rewarding players for staying at low health in a classic high-risk, high-reward playstyle.

Rogue and Hacker revolved around dodge builds, often combined with critical hits and suppressed weapons.

In Payday 3, that level of variety has almost completely disappeared.

Always Online

This is, in my opinion, the game's biggest flaw.

text:
Review: A promising game covered in diarrhea.
(I played the game by “sailing the seas” method for 3 years. I finally bought this just to write this review, and I bought it at full price out of pity, not because it earned it.)

Good Side:
=========

This game genuinely feels like an upgrade from my beloved Payday 2. The graphics, guns, animations, and sounds all just click, and I love that part of it. Base heists are somewhat fun, and the AI pathfinding and difficulty scaling have improved a lot compared to the last game. The stealth system feels more readable and less janky in some situations, and when it works, it actually feels smoother than PD2.
title: PAYDAY 3 — review 224623804

text:
I also like the vendor system, it gives a proper underworld black market vibe. Skills are fairly balanced and not completely broken like some PD2 builds used to be. Gunplay overall feels heavier and more grounded, and the hit feedback is genuinely satisfying when the game isn’t busy tripping over itself.

Bad Side:
========

Oh boy, there’s a lot of shjt to unpack here. First and biggest issue is the complete lack of offline mode. Payday has always been a co-op shooter, but requiring a live server was never a necessity. Starbreeze forced this online-only crap down everyone’s throat. People begged for offline mode, got promises, waited years, and then got hit with “not feasible.” That’s not just a middle finger to your core player base, it’s a self-inflicted death sentence for preservation and long-term playability.

But let’s be honest, did it work? No. Your servers are barely more secure than a school computer lab. People have been playing this game and its DLCs for free anyway (including myself). And optimization, or whatever you want to call it, is another mess. Yes, it’s UE4, but that’s not an excuse. Plenty of UE4 games run significantly better. The performance feels unpolished, unstable, and inconsistent even on hardware that should easily handle it.

PAYDAY 3 takes a giant step away from its predecessor... and falls down the stairs, Peter Griffin style.

Is the game fun to play when it works? Kinda. The game got better after the release with the introduction of reworked (PAYDAY 2-like) armor and skill systems. Stealth got more mechanically complicated with the introduction of different types of zones (Public, Private, and Secure), different types of civilians (normal Pedestrians and Employees), and the new Search phase that is now triggered first before the alarm (which throws out of the window all timings and paths of guards, so you have to be much more careful). And switching the difficulty feels more impactful than in the 2nd part, where playing on Mayhem is pretty much the same as on Death Sentence.

text:
I played the beta and didn't like it at the time due to severe connection issues, but honestly, this game is improving a lot. If the developers keep at it, this could easily become the next No Man's Sky style comeback story.

The good:

-The heists are cool and have really good theme variations.
-The animations are top-tier; movement and actions feel incredibly fluid, realistic, and well-done.
-The new gameplay mechanics are a very welcome change of pace.
-The new assault system feels way more natural and realistic. For example, when the police first arrive, they actually try to negotiate with you, unlike Payday 2 where a Bulldozer would teleport into the bank two seconds after the alarm rang.
title: PAYDAY 3 — review 229819522

text:
-There aren't many masks available yet, but the designs they do have look great.
-The objectives feel way less repetitive because they stopped overusing those constant drill repairs from Payday 2.

The bad:

-The game needs more heists. There are currently fewer than 20, and for a game built entirely around replayability, you need way more variation.
-Progression feels completely lacking. The devs still seem clueless on how to handle it, and adding an infamy or "prestige" system with exclusive rewards would be a massive improvement.
-There are only four difficulty levels and they aren't particularly challenging, so the game needs more bite. A "realistic" mode with fewer cops but much higher enemy damage would be perfect.

text: I have been playing Payday since the original Payday: the Heist, and it has to be said, while I do suggest this game for those who enjoy the heist subgenre, this unfortunately comes with some caveats. Payday 3 is an evolution of the series, but not in an entirely positive way. The game's core systems are effective, but pared back in a way that makes objectives feel a lot more uniform than in payday 2, which limits heist replayability, something that is very important for a game that relies on that very replayability as a core element of it's gameplay loop. With that said, I find both the stealth and shooting mechanics to be much more reliable, which wins it some solid points.
title: PAYDAY 3 — review 214110651

text:
The new upgrade system likewise has been simplified (no more weapon part packages for one), making it much easier to build your weapons as you'd like without the randomisation factor, but that simplicity is let down somewhat by how opaque things are. It's great that I'm not jumping through hoops, but that doesn't help me if i don't have a solid idea of what the green and red bars actually mean practically in a heist.

In short, the game has been streamlined and modernized. The problem is, that has come at the cost of, well, long-term game-health. Personally, I still enjoy the game enough to regularly play it, particularly since the devs do seem determined to fix the issues and get back on steady footing; but it is hard to ignore that Payday 2 is just a better game at the moment, multiple years on.

text:
I understand why so many players are disappointed with Payday 3. It’s not a bad game, and I actually appreciate how easy it is to get into. You level up quickly, the systems are simple, and it’s clearly beginner-friendly. However, that accessibility mostly exists because Payday 3 offers far less depth than Payday 2. There are significantly fewer weapons, skill trees, and overall customization options. In fact, it sometimes feels even more barebones than Payday: The Heist, and that’s a serious problem.

The gameplay itself also feels outdated, like playing a game from around 2015 rather than a modern sequel. Melee attacks feel useless, and the skill trees lack impact and power, making progression feel underwhelming instead of rewarding.
title: PAYDAY 3 — review 217361444

The Good;

-Fresher take on Stealth as civilian mode allows for a more flexible playstyle and less black/white builds, doable even with loud-focused setups and flows nicely into the alarms going off.

-Generally satisfying weapon handling and visual customization, although their mechanical modification still needs a rework to be less abstract, for which small steps have been recently taken, such as the introduction of damage numbers in Options.

-Fleshed out mask customization by parts instead of as a whole, to the point of being reverse ported to PD2, however comes with the caveat of having to randomly drops the best looking paints on level up, which would be fixed by allowing their purchase with C-Stacks.

text:

-Lack of inventory management, one would think that dragging and dropping and reordering items/clothes/masks/weapons would be common sense in 2026, but it's not at the time of writing this.

text:
Gameplay and Police Assaults:

The gunplay is satisfying enough; headshots actually pop, and the movement feels really nice. Doing objectives and watching unique animations on doing them is very rewarding. Heists are different enough, but it's missing a bit of uniqueness. Like it feels like every heist ends with escaping the cops with a bike in a chopper the majority of the time or twitching in his usual van spot. But I've seen them trying to be different with The Shopping Spree Heist having a unique escape and cutscene, which is a nod to L4D2 Dead Center.

But the special enemies still act similar to Payday 2. Tasers/Zappers tase you, Shields are much more reactive and actually benefit the swats and synergize with them well, and Bulldozers are a big threat without any shotgun or overkill anti-dozer weapons. Snipers actually snipe you.

6/10. Youngblood is the experimental spin-off of the modern era, focusing on co-op gameplay starring B.J.'s twin daughters.

If you are playing this with a friend, it is a decent, brainless co-op shooter. However, if you are playing solo, the AI companion can be incredibly frustrating. The game introduces light RPG elements, level-gated zones, and enemy health/armor bars which completely changes the classic Wolfenstein pacing into a bit of a grind. It’s not terrible, but it's definitely the weakest link in the modern lineup.

Pros:
+ Fun co-op mechanics and level progression if you have a dedicated partner.
+ Level design by Arkane Studios (Dishonored) makes exploring Paris feel very open and vertical.

Cons:
- Enemy level-gating and bullet-spongy health bars ruin the fast-paced power fantasy of the franchise.
- Solo play is severely hindered by mediocre friendly AI.

Previous entries established a certain standard, and you'd reasonably expect a new installment to at least attempt to meet that standard. Well, here we are. The newest installment of the Wolfenstein franchise.

As I've gotten all the other games from a bundle, I blindly went into this one despite the criticism I've seen it receive. First thing to note is Co-op. Didn't know they would attempt to do something like Portal 2's co-op in a Nazi-killing game but okay.

I had to host a private game because single player is apparently non-existent unless you count dragging around a bot partner that seems to have been trained exclusively to stand in the wrong place.

Then comes gameplay. Played only the first mission (took about 30 minutes), and the entire game has been watered down into some RPG-styled shooter where everything revolves around powering yourself up and watching the numbers go up.
