text:
But more importantly, it changes the feeling of actually killing enemies. In the previous games, clearing an area could involve actual planning, like figuring out where the commanders were, whether to stay quiet or go loud, picking off enemies without alerting others and getting that satisfying feeling when the whole area had been cleared because you actually executed your approach properly.

This is all gone, replaced with entering an area, shooting whatever is in front of you, moving towards the next objective and repeat. Stealth feels less meaningful and killing enemies starts to feel like something you do because the game put them there rather than because you made an interesting decision about how to deal with them.

Even The New Colossus, despite being significantly more exaggerated and ridiculous than The New Order, still had serious moments and enough worldbuilding to make the story feel grounded.

Youngblood feels like The New Colossus was taken apart, all the recognizable pieces were put into a blender and someone decided the missing pieces could be replaced with RPG mechanics. Less of a continuation of the series and more like someone made a completely different game and remembered halfway through development that they had the Wolfenstein license.

If you're getting it as part of a bundle with the other games, sure the other titles make the price worth it. But buying Youngblood by itself? I'd rather just replay The New Order.

I do not care how aristocratic one pretends to be, those infernal mechanical hounds make ones skin crawl. The noises they make, along with the unholy groans of the Ubersoldaten, sound profoundly unnatural, as though Satan himself had developed a fascination with industrial farts. I also adore the many enemy variants. They keep every encounter fresh and ensure one never grows too comfortable. Except for the kamikaze hounds. I despise those explosive little bastards with every fibre of my thoroughly aristocratic being. May they kindly take their final fart elsewhere.

The guns remain as gloriously chunky as ever. Wolfenstein has always understood that firearms should feel less like weapons and more like portable declarations of war.

If you're a fan of the Wolfenstein universe, Youngblood is a solid side mission worth taking. It’s not a traditional entry like The New Order or The New Colossus, but it still delivers that signature Nazi-blasting action with a co-op twist.

👍 Pros
- Fast-paced gunplay with satisfying weapons
- Cool alternate-history Paris setting
- Co-op mode adds a fresh dynamic (especially fun with a friend)
- Plenty of callbacks and lore for longtime fans

👎 Cons
- Story feels lighter and less impactful than previous titles
- AI companion can be hit-or-miss
- RPG elements (like level gating) might not be everyone's cup of tea

The Blazkowicz twins bring a different energy - more youthful, more banter - but once you settle into the rhythm, it’s a fun ride. Not groundbreaking, but definitely not bad. If you love the universe, you’ll find enough here to enjoy.

text:
RECOMMENDED IF YOU CAN GET IT ON SALE. I got this for a few dollars, really only to complete my modern Wolfenstein collection, but overall I had a good time. I am not 100% done with the game yet, but I have gotten a good way through. Here's a breakdown:

Audio: The audio sounds great. The footsteps, ammo pickups, and weapon sounds are satisfying.

Gunplay: I enjoyed the gunplay a lot, especially with the mod system on the guns, bringing more depth to combat styles. The guns are not pinpoint accurate like in the other games, which I like. This gives value to trigger control for some guns and the accuracy stat.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 230383424

text:
This gives value to trigger control for some guns and the accuracy stat.

Story: Pretty much a suggestion. It's one of those games that if you're playing for the story you'll be disappointed. That's probably the worse part of this game. The story feels like it has zero weight to it. The Nazis are just copy paste generic bad guys. The dialog can be very tedious in game and there is almost zero character depth. There's a quest system bundled in that lets you progress at your own pace. You can either send the main missions immediately and get to the story fast or progress more through side missions and see all of the maps more.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 230383424

text:
Combat: I liked the feel of the combat, but the introduction of health bars is very controversial. It removes a lot of the suspense behind bosses and larger enemies, because you know exactly how much more you need to shoot them. The stealth isn't bad, it's just very unnecessary. While I am split on the health bars, I really like the armor type system. It makes it so you can't just pick one gun and spray every enemy you see.

Immersion: This game lacks real immersion like the other entries in the modern Wolfenstein franchise. I think this is due to the visual style, health bars, and companion system. Other than those items it is hard to put my finger on why it lacks the immersion.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 230383424

Performance and Graphics: I had no performance issues, the game ran well and looks great.

Overall: This game is fun little arcade shooter that is definitely worth it if you can get it on sale. While there are definitely negatives, and things that are worse that Wolfenstein 2, it's hard to compete with that game, and I can never rag on a studio for trying something new instead of just copy-pasting their old games. TL;DR:
"If you buy what the game actually sells to you ... then you can expect to get somewhat of 50 hours of fun and joy" [Consider that the game at the time of this review sells for ~3.5€ in online retailers]

Where I Come From:
I ended up playing this game as part of a full series run I did for my channel after playing back to back Return To Castle Wolfenstein, Wolfenstein 2009, The Old Blood, The New Order and The New Colossus.

What The Game IS and what it sell to you:
As a game comes as a sandbox-y spin off continuation of the events which took place in The New Colossus and it delivers it really well to the extend it is meant to, for the type of game it is.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 216188496

text:
It is not a live Service game, so it is meant to be consumed up to the point in which what you actually do into the game is objectified and has a meaning (expect that to happen close to 50hours mark if you play it in Challenging Difficulty and Solo as I did). It is by all means logical for it to start feeling repetitive after moving beyond that mark if you choose to go after the steam challenges etc.
It is designed mainly to be played as a coop and it is leaning towards a more "arcade-ish" and more "light/Fun" oriented experience ... and it delivers on that front.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 216188496

text:
and it delivers on that front.

Lets break it down a bit now :)

STORY (Smart/Legit):
For the type of game it is (and meant to be), the story serves mostly as a means to an end but it does NOT do that by derailing the actual story of the series, on the contrary it offers a perspective of a possible future in which literally the Youngblood comes on the front and makes IT theirs, continuing the saga of the main characters and events. We witness a future in which the kids (of the new colossus) are curated by their parents to take their place moving forward as aging is unavoidable even for BJ Anya and Grace.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 216188496

text:
Now if you know the story of the series well you will realize that the story of the game not only is Smart but it also aims to fill all the gaps left open at the end of the New Colossus (I am not going to spoil). On top of that I believe that if you pay attention the game Hints also the direction we should expect to witness in Wolfenstein 3 when it comes out.

Graphics (In some occasions even better than the main games):
It might be a spin off and everything I said thus far, but the game delivers really good and detailed graphics and you can clearly see that they did not cut corners when they were creating every single inch of the areas and the LODs.
title: Wolfenstein: Youngblood — review 216188496

text:
Sound (Really Good):
The atmosphere is spot on, the guns sound like actual guns (and not like if you are playing Star Trek). The immersion techniques of the series are present and smart and over all not only it does not fall short but in some cases it adds up on what we have seen so far from the main titles.

Gameplay (Fluent and Joyful):
All known mechanics are here and improved on top of some smart additions. Nothing special to point out here.

Noteworthy Mentions:
You can not out-level the enemies.
The world adapts to your level dynamically.
Quick match coop is completely Pepega ... the game is better played coop with a friend.
Ai is legit and unforgiving in challenging.

text:
Dawn of Wa…sted potential

I wish there was a mixed option for reviews, because this is not completely horrible, but it has so many issues and it’s such an enormous downgrade on both previous DoW games that I simply cannot give this a positive review.

The main points I’d like to address:

- Dawn of War III takes some mechanics from the first two games and tries combining them into a hybridy RTS amalgam, but the result is structurally different from either predecessor. It restores permanent base buildings, tech structures, and unit production similar to Dawn of War I, but the number of structures and upgrades is reduced.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text:
It restores permanent base buildings, tech structures, and unit production similar to Dawn of War I, but the number of structures and upgrades is reduced. Movement on most maps is limited to straight lanes though, literally MOBA-style for some reason, which is so out of place and horrible that it's astonishing to me that they’d even try combining MOBA elements with classic RTS. Insanely horrible decision. Army management is built around three tiers of infantry, vehicles, and super-units, with a smaller overall roster per faction than in the earlier games. There are also only 3 factions - Space Marines, Eldar and Orks.

- From Dawn of War II, it adopts hero-style “Elite Units” with active abilities and short cooldowns. These Elites function as high-impact pieces that anchor most engagements, and their abilities often decide fights more than standard troops.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text: These Elites function as high-impact pieces that anchor most engagements, and their abilities often decide fights more than standard troops. Cover, suppression, and retreat mechanics from Dawn of War II are removed. Instead, the game emphasizes constant forward pressure, objective control points, and destroying shield generators to reach the enemy core. All multiplayer matches use this single victory structure. To me, the elites seem like an attempt to copy Warcraft/Starcraft, and it definitely didn’t end up great. The heroes are fine, they quite literally play the exact same way the ones in Warcraft/Starcraft do, but with way less abilities. I just do not understand why they tried to do that, like, the previous games had some focus on hero units, they should’ve expanded on that rather than try forcing something that doesn’t belong.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text: - The campaign alternates between Space Marines, Eldar, and Orks in a fixed mission order (you basically play one mission as one race, then another, then the third race, and so on). Such multi-perspective narration could work, if done right, but the writing and narration in this is absolutely abysmal, so it just feels like it's forced for the sake of chronologic storytelling. The voice acting is also desperate. They tried connecting the story to the first DoW, especially with the returning characters, and I’m genuinely sorry that they did, because it’s not very good, so it feels like spitting in the face of the first legendary DoW. And I still can’t get over fkin Orks with a British slangy accent thing. Like, wtf?
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text:
Like, wtf?

- Missions use linear objectives and scripted encounters rather than the dynamic army-building of Dawn of War I or the small-squad progression of Dawn of War II. Resource income is tied to captured points, and expansion is straightforward without requisition/power generators or wargear systems from the earlier titles. And resource generation is painfully slow, to the point that you at times literally have to sit and wait for resources to trickle in. Gameplay-wise and story-wise, throughout the entire campaign I genuinely had the impression that my intelligence was being insulted with how idiotic some things were.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text:
- The soundtrack and general vibe of the game are also just horribly lacking in every possible way. When you compare that to the feeling of epicness and grandeur you get in the first DoW, this here can't even be considered luke warm. Nothing makes you feel even 1% of that, because the soundtrack you don't even notice, voice acting is unenergetic and uncoherent, most missions are just bland moba-style 1v1s with some few scripted events in-between, etc. Literally nothing to get you excited, let alone convey a feeling of epicness.

- There are quite a lot of weird interactions and bugs, some of which are not exactly minor. One example, when you beat certain campaign missions, you unlock some sort of profile pictures or whatever.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text:
One example, when you beat certain campaign missions, you unlock some sort of profile pictures or whatever. The next time you open the game, it displays these in a window in the middle of your screen, with you having to press „Ok“ to close the window. Problem is, it doesn't work. You can spam clicks on the „Ok“ as much as you want, but the window won't close, and you can't proceed, meaning your only option is alt+f4 and open the game again. Not the worst thing, but, like, seriously bruh?

Overall, Dawn of War III is mechanically somewhat faster and more ability-driven than the first game, with more traditional RTS elements than the second, but it is also less specialized than either of them, especially with the addition of the MOBA-like elements.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 211486578

text: If you don’t compare it to the previous two DoW games, I guess this could be considered an OKish Warhammer 40k game that’s just a weird mixture of different genre elements, but even with that, it’s just definitely not a very good Dawn of War game. The resulting game sits between several of those styles without fully matching the depth of either of them. It’s actually astonishing that the developers had both previous games as template and years of player feedback on both, and then they somehow ended up missing to the point that you have to ask yourself: wtf is wrong with these people, do they not understand their own game(s)?

text:
I got this in a heavily discounted bundle and avoided it for a long time because nobody I knew had anything good to say about it. I finally got around to installing it and seeing for myself.

Is it a bad game? No. Is it a bad Dawn of War game? Very much so.

Had they made this a stand alone game with a new franchise title people might not have been so outraged by it. That being said, it feels and plays like a MOBA or cell phone game. Lets just get straight to how it differs from previous games and why it ultimately fails.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 206178378

text:
Lets just get straight to how it differs from previous games and why it ultimately fails.

The bad
---------
* Too much ♥♥♥♥ going on in every fight. There's no good keybinding controls to switch between your units, aside from your hero, so by the time you cycle between them to pop off abilities the fight is already over or units are already dead. I have never used most of the abilities, because it's been easier to just make a giant deathball of troops and steamroll enemy units with them.
* The base building mechanics are pretty needless since all the maps are just linear pathways. They could have just taken a lesson from DoW 2 and focused on minor reinforcements at various progression points and skipped the needless resource mechanics entirely.
* One campaign that alternates between the factions.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 206178378

text:
This is probably the dumbest thing they could have done. In Warhammer players favor certain factions. There is already not enough missions to go around in the campaign. Further wasting time by making players play factions they don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about should have warranted someone in the design team getting fired. The whole point of campaigns is to give players the ability to grow into and adapt to the play style of a faction over time by posing different challenges in each mission.
* Pointless set dressing. Maps are riddled with explosive barrels and medkits that are worthless. These features cannot be directly targeted or interacted with, usually you have to use a special ability like an area attack over them to destroy them, and even then I think they're just there for visual effects because I don't think they've actually done any damage to any units.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 206178378

text:
Medkits have to be walked over by wounded units but they're always placed behind walls of enemies or so far off the beaten path that you have to take guys out of the fight to grab them, so they're pretty useless when you need them. In revious games they were an inventory charge item, or could be clicked on.

The Good - but not enough to save it
-----------
* Music is fantastic.
* Cutscenes and Art design are several leaps forward from previous games.

Much has been said about this game. Mostly negative. I always thought that the outrage about it seems a little exaggerated, and a lot of it truly is. I mean, a lot of people are freaking out about the Space Marine commander being able to jump, others complain that the units look too clean and colorful, etc. Most of these complaints sound silly to me.

I jumped into it with an open mind.

Played three campaign missions. They taught you basics of each faction, but were still actual missions. I can't say for sure whether the campaign would continue to feel like these missions, but they felt kinda boring to me. They were mostly linear, usually giving you no more than two ways to solve each situation, and the enemies were very passive.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 235136068

text:
They were mostly linear, usually giving you no more than two ways to solve each situation, and the enemies were very passive.

The Space Marine one was the simplest, you just keep going forward and attacking the enemies. The Ork one forced you to defend this gun, which I thought was lame. The Eldar one was a piece of cake. Why? You're pretty much not getting attacked, so you're free to develop at you own pace. Then once you get the aviation, just build a giant squadron and send it over to each tower you need to destroy. I've said this before, but why do we need aviation in Dawn of War? It ruins the whole dynamic of inching your way through the map, capturing strategic points and fortifying, when you can just fly over everything.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 235136068

text:
It ruins the whole dynamic of inching your way through the map, capturing strategic points and fortifying, when you can just fly over everything.

I will say that there are many things I really liked about DoW3. I think it's cool how Orks can upgrade their units by finding scrap and how the Eldar are very reliant on staying within the fields of their web ways. I really liked the maps visually. They convey the sense of scale and depth really well. I like how the new cover system too, it makes the covers more valuable as advantageous spots on the map that you compete with the enemy for. I also like how you can build requisition and power generators alongside each other on the same spot.

text:

However, the campaign is really the last thing I'm interested in (unless it's Dark Crusade's campaign). I was much more curious about the skirmish mode. And this is where things went to ♥♥♥♥ for me really quickly.

I don't really have any fundamental problem with the gameplay in theory. I think it works more or less similar to the original DoW, except the big things is you can't replenish your forces unless you're near your main buildings. But I was getting my ass handed to me on casual difficulty. Why? Because my units kept acting like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. And this is to me the one problem that absolutely handicaps DoW3. I can't leave my units to defend a post and then focus on other things.

text:
The hate for this game is just ridiculous. It seems like some people are unable to formulate their own opinions and instead jump straight on the bandwagon.

As someone who has played Dawn of War 1 and 2, including all of their DLC, and has accumulated hundreds of hours across both games, I honestly find that Dawn of War 3 differs far less from its predecessors than people make it out to.

Dawn of War 3 offers an interesting campaign and introduces the ability to play as multiple factions throughout the story, rather than sticking with the same Blood Ravens narrative. It also retains many of the core mechanics that made the previous games enjoyable, including base building, unit upgrades, base upgrades, capture points, unit tier systems, and much more.

My only real complaints with the game are the occasional crash and some dialogue occasionally being out of sync with the character’s facial animations. Beyond that, I find a lot of the complaints about the game’s overall state to be exaggerated. Boycotting the game simply because, for once, you had to kill Space Marines is especially asinine. The Classic Blunder - Doing too much, for the Sake of Doing It

It always baffles me why game developers decide to take away key features or functions of a game that made it such a memorable and amazing time for players. The gaming industry has a serious problem, and that's game developers feeling the need to do more, or do the most, or change things, or take out mechanics or features of a game that made it the hit that it was.

I don't know if it's upper management putting pressure on the team to innovate and press the boundaries, or if it's simply a lack of insight and a severe case of short-sightedness. At any rate, what we see in many games today, and indeed from this latest Warhammer installment, is another classic example of that.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 218178795

text:
At any rate, what we see in many games today, and indeed from this latest Warhammer installment, is another classic example of that.

Reduced base building, over-simplified resource management, and perhaps the most frustrating of all, the lack of the ability to destroy a unit once it is created, makes this game a mere shadow of what it could have been. Game developers need to understand, embrace, and accept that sometimes the best formula for creating an awesome sequel is by simply adding a few cool new features to a framework that already succeeded.

For example, Grand Theft Auto San Andreas was probably the greatest Grand Theft Auto title of its time because it took the exact same formula that it had built upon from Grand Theft Auto 3 and Vice City and added some awesome cool features like airplanes, parachutes, etc.

text:
Review: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III

Dawn of War III tries to mix the styles of the first two games — classic RTS and hero-focused battles — but doesn’t fully succeed at either. You control Space Marines, Eldar, and Orks fighting over a powerful artifact called the Spear of Khaine. The campaign switches between all three factions and offers some good variety in missions.

Visually, the game looks great. Battles are huge, explosions fill the screen, and units feel powerful. The soundtrack and voice acting fit the Warhammer 40K tone well. Watching elite units like Gabriel Angelos or giant Ork war machines tear through enemies is satisfying.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 207714563

text:
Gameplay, however, is divisive. It focuses too much on hero units and special abilities, making it feel closer to a MOBA than a traditional strategy game. Base-building and large army management take a back seat. Older fans who loved the tactical freedom of Dawn of War II or the scale of the original might find this one too simplified.

Multiplayer is fast and flashy but lacks depth and map variety. The campaign is decent once, but replay value is limited. The game was supported for a while, then updates stopped, so it feels like a finished but abandoned project.

Overall, Dawn of War III looks and sounds great but sacrifices depth for spectacle. It’s worth playing on sale if you want cinematic sci-fi battles, but not if you’re looking for a classic RTS experience.

Despite its bad reputation, this will always be my first game from the Warhammer 40k universe. Three years ago it didn’t pull me into the fandom, but now, after finishing the previous games in the series, I replayed the whole campaign — this time on hard difficulty.

Back then and even now, I’d still say it’s definitely not a bad game. On the contrary, the campaign is fun and can keep you engaged for around 18 hours. The story has nice cutscenes and a solid atmosphere. It’s a little disappointing that the three races (Space Marines, Orks, and Eldar) rotate in every mission, so you don’t really get to choose who you want to play as. Because of that, my favorite Blood Ravens only get about 5 missions, which isn’t much. Missions are long (around 1 hour each) and vary between defending, capturing points, building bases, and hero-only sections.

- In this MOBA game, they have base buildings and allow you to build buildings anywhere on the map.

- You can build and command multiple units in this MOBA game, and there are no uncontrollable creep units that auto-spawn toward the enemy base.

- You capture strategic points to generate resources—not from killing minions/creeps or jungle creeps—just like in MOBA games.

By this point, I can call Unreal Tournament's Onslaught mode and other similar lane-pushing mechanics a MOBA game too, without even mentioning how game mechanics can be inspired by other games.

text:
The infamous Dawn of War 3: Better than its reputation but clearly the weakest part in the series.

The story: A warp-traveling planet with a powerful Eldar artefact is about to arrive and Eldar and Orks both want to claim the artefact for themselves while the Imperium wants to keep it from them. You got all the clichés of a Warhammer story: Scheming backstabbing Eldar, Orks on a WAAAGH! Looking for loot, incompetent Inquisitors who make everything worse, Space Marines who defiles orders due to honour and in the end the different factions need to work together to fight a bigger evil. In my opinion it’s all a bit too much.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 210079979

text:
In my opinion it’s all a bit too much.

The gameplay: The game tries to find the middle ground between classic RTS of Dawn of War 1 and the powerful heroes and micromanagement of Dawn of War 2. The end result is a bit like DoW 2 Retribution but with a bit of base building and bigger armies.

The campaign is diversified with a lot of different objectives and shared between all three factions. Unfortunately this means you constantly switch between them and it makes it more difficult to learn the faction specific mechanics. Orks for example can use the scrap left by destroyed buildings and vehicles to upgrade their troops or construct new vehicles cheap. Eldars have regenerating energy shields and can teleport their builds and troops which favour a hit-and-run tactics.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 210079979

text:
Eldars have regenerating energy shields and can teleport their builds and troops which favour a hit-and-run tactics.

Multiplayer comes with practically two game modes. Simply destroy everything with or without defensive towers and the objective based mode “Power Core”. Here the players have to destroy one after another a shield generator, then a defensive gun and finally the eponymous power core in the enemy base all while defending your own versions of those structures. The mode is actually quite clever since especially the defensive gun prevents early game rushes while most maps allow for sneak attacks on the structures.

The problems: It’s quite obvious Dawn of War 1 and 2 were developed by fans of the Warhammer 40 setting. The same thing can’t be said about part 3.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 210079979

text:
The same thing can’t be said about part 3. Gabriel Angelos jumping around in heavy Terminator armour like he is Thor from Marvel looks as ridiculous as is sounds. Bolters sound terrible as if they simply copied the machine gun sound from Company of Heroes. Melee units die fairly easily but you can’t completely ignore them because you need them to dislodge the enemies form shield bubbles, the only thing left from the cover-system. The missing sync kills is especially obvious in commando-missions without base building.

Like I said before DoW 3 tries to appeal to the fans of both predecessor and only manages to alienate both sides. Those who wanted Dawn of War 1 will be annoyed by the ridiculously strong elite units (the heroes) and the micro-management of the abilities of both the elite and normal units.
title: Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — review 210079979

text:
Fans of Dawn of War 2 will miss the customisation of the elite units and notice the wide swing in the power of the elite units. Some are overpowered and win fights practically by themselves and others are barely more powerful than two normal infantry squads.

I can’t stop wondering what the game might have been if developer and publisher didn’t drop the support after a few months. Still the campaign is okay and skirmish can helps scratch this Warhammer-40K-itch until Part 4 is released.
